text:
🛡️ AI security is now a global conversation. For agents, one question sits at the center: who decides what they are allowed to do?

Recent reports from top AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropoic describe evaluation agents gaining unauthorized access to real systems. These were research settings with reduced safeguards, not ordinary consumer sessions. Our takeaway: model behavior and enforceable access controls both matter.

🏡 At home, this becomes personal. An agent connected to your information, devices and services needs boundaries you can understand and change.

That is central to AgentKeys, the home agent manager we're building for individuals and families.

🪪 Each agent has its own identity and approved access. Giving one agent permission does not give every other agent the same access.

✅ You choose what it can read and use, and you can revoke that access. Permission checks sit outside the AI: a model can request more access, but cannot approve that request itself.

🔐 Personal content stays in encrypted storage off-chain. Heima records permissions and audit proofs, not the contents of your household documents.

The first version of the application framework has landed in the codebase. These controls are one layer of defense, not a claim that AgentKeys eliminates every AI-security risk.

💬 Which permissions would you want to review before letting an agent act for you?

text:
An underrated opportunity right now is figuring out how to measure subjective agent work.

Crypto has historically relied on objective mechanisms such as:

- Proof-of-Work to prove computational work was expended
- Validity rules to determine whether transactions and state transitions follow the protocol
- Slashing to penalise provable misbehaviour like double-signing

None of these mechanisms measure whether a buyer received what they intended to purchase. 

We have some infrastructure for resolving bespoke disputes, but we do not have sufficient infrastructure for determining whether a scoped job completed by an agent actually met a buyer's expectations at scale.

Existing approaches solve adjacent problems such as:

@Kleros_io and @UMAprotocol - can adjudicate disputes but rely on human participation and is designed for infrequent disputes

@bittensor - evaluates miner performance within subnets, not whether a buyer's intent was executed

@virtuals_io - has evaluator agents, but evaluators are selected per task and there are no economic guarantees tied to the outcomes (yet)

A missing primitive that is yet to be built is a way for two agents that do not trust each other to scope a job, agree on conditions for success, execute the work, evaluate the outcome and release payment at scale.

Lots of open questions around how to build this, such as how to:

- Resolve disputes at machine speed
- Keep sensitive information private during negotiation and evaluation
- Prevent collusion between agents using the same model providers
- Evaluate outcomes where quality is subjective
- Determine who bears cost when agent fails

In general, I think liability will be important here. If agents have capital and/or reputation at stake, they can be penalised when they fail to deliver against clearly specified commitments.

I do think pricing the risk is hard though. In saying that, if a protocol can accurately price the probability that an agent delivers a specified outcome and that pricing improves with every buyer–seller interaction, it will become more valuable over time. The data could be used to build a kind of matchmaking moat, e.g. understanding which agents reliably deliver which outcomes for which buyers.

It's an early space but I expect mechanisms for evaluating subjective agent work will be critically needed soon. As agents take on more economically valuable work and expect to be paid for it, we will need a way for two agents that don't trust each other to agree on when a job is done.

author: Stacks
quoted_text:
Started testing a looping strategy on @ZestProtocol to farm some of their new incentive campaign.

Here's what I've been doing:

• Supplied ~$92 of $sBTC
• Borrowed 30 $USDCx against it
• Swapped the USDCx into more $sBTC
• Supplied that sBTC back into Zest
• Repeated with another 10 $USDCx

Final position:

• $133 $sBTC supplied
• 40 $USDCx debt
• $93 net equity

Zest is now paying 0.5 BTC per month in incentives in $STX.

Half goes to $sBTC suppliers, while the other half goes to $USDCx borrowers with 20%+ LTV.

So the loop potentially lets me increase my sBTC exposure while earning incentives on both the supply and borrow side.

Of course, leverage cuts both ways.

A 10% rise in sBTC adds roughly $13 to my supplied position before interest and fees. A 10% drop does the opposite while also pushing my LTV higher.

Anyone running other loops on Zest?

Disclosure: I’m a long-time Stacks supporter and $STX holder.

TODAY, everything changes, period!

People keep acting like cloture is a favor to crypto bros and billionaires, guess what? It isn’t. It’s actually a rulebook for for the everyday hard working souls who already got burned.

Right now you can “own” an asset, lose the exchange, and find out in court you only owned a claim. That’s not innovation. That’s a loophole with a logo. Regular people eat the loss and the corrupt who built the mess lawyer up.

The CLARITY Act just says the obvious out loud: you can hold your own keys, customer funds aren’t the company’s piggy bank, and fraud doesn’t get a hall pass because it happened on-chain. Americans shouldn’t have to guess which regulator notices them after the fact.

A yes on cloture doesn’t pass the bill. It lets the Senate debate it like adults without the virtue signaling and false hysteria. A no doesn’t protect Main Street. It protects the gray zone, and that’s exactly where the next FTX lurks.

text:
First week of @Alphaschool South Bay LA is in the books for my three kids. I'm super impressed already, but I drank the Koolaid long ao. Here's a spattering of updates if you're interested.
* Transparency - night and day between this summer. We were honestly scared the location search would die, but now that school is open, the comms from the school is almost overwhelming. And, through Timeback, I'm already tracking daily learning.
* Earn everything - I've heard this multiple times from my kids this week. They are blown away by what they can earn, but realize they have to earn it. My middle daughter came home one day and immediately told me she wanted to make goals with her guide so she could earn a set of headphones that's available.
* Field trips - The kids were informed they will go on 50-60 field trips this year, which 3-4 on domestic flights, and 1 Int'l. All, only if earned. The 1st field trip happened on day 4!
* MAP testing only in mornings so far, so no screen learning yet. Setting a baseline. My son tested at 99% on Math 8th grade MAP test, while my 7th grade daughter tested at 3rd grade science and reading. Both don't really care...they know that all that matters is how well they improve from here.
* The Playa Vista building is huge and decked out. Kids and guides are planning use of all sorts of empty rooms (they have to earn each) - 3d printer room, woodworking room, gaming room, movie room, garden, drone room, futsol field/team/room, maker space room, art room, science lab, etc.
* "How was school?" All 3 kids are already responding "good, great, fun". Huge step up from last years' answers "boring, sucks, ugh". 
* Enrollment: 25 kids a week before school, now already at 28. (I believe we'll be at 60-100 by year end.) No complaints about the number of kids of friends or anything like that yet.
* Carpools are amazing already. Interesting conversations among kids K-8. Partially just great kids, partially due to their excitement around school. 10x better than previous year carpools.
* First workshop is learning to surf, 2x/wk. Learning independence, goals, tools, safety, grit, etc.

我盘算了一下，大概就是五件事，但这五件事都是在打川普的脸：

1. 从伊朗撤走美军，也就是解封伊朗港口，但解封伊朗港口未必伊朗就会解封霍尔木兹，如果伊朗仍然没有解封，就相当于美国单方面受罪，伊朗可以重新进出口石油。

2. 美国解除对伊朗的经济制裁，这对于刚刚才开始“弃婴行动”来说，目标就是进一步切断伊朗的金融、贸易和能源收入，而且 9 月还在继续扩大制裁。

3. 解冻伊朗被冻结的海外资产，这对川普来说可能是最简单最没有压力的一件事了，虽然也会打脸，但相比其它的要轻很多。

4. 给伊朗战争赔偿或者重新拿出重建资金。这一条可能是最难看的。伊朗现在已经公开把赔偿列入重新开放霍尔木兹的条件之一。这次不管怎么说都是妥妥的战争赔款了。

5. 停止战争，重新接受伊朗控制下的霍尔木兹通行方案。说人话就是接受伊朗对霍尔木兹收费，这脸打的也很响，毕竟川普多次表示霍尔木兹不可能收费。

所以虽然我在做空石油，但我觉得让川普 TACO 的概率还是有点低，反而是包括中国在内对伊朗施压，让伊朗开放部分霍尔木兹航线还稍微有点可能，毕竟现在也是在加重包括中国在内对伊朗友好国家的通胀。

说实话，最近做空石油确实让我有些焦虑了。

焦虑的并不是石油的价格上涨，我准备金都是到 120 美元的，而且即便是 120 美元不够，拉到 150 美元都没啥问题，所以我焦虑的从来都不是方向。

其次是全球对伊朗的态度，霍尔木兹的封锁带来的并不仅仅是美国油价的上涨，还是全球油价和通胀的上涨，即便是中国，石油战略储备已经突破天际了，但仍然因为伊朗港口的封锁而上涨油价。

现在反而是全球都被伊朗给钳制了，号称军事实力第一的美国没有把伊朗打服，全球第二大经济体的中国也因为霍尔木兹而束手无措。

如果只是油价涨到 100、110，甚至 120 美元，对我的仓位来说都只是浮亏的问题，只要保证金足够，我可以继续等。

截至目前在凌晨清晰法案终止动议投票前有两件关键因素导致市场预期投票成功率下降：

This post has garnered a lot of attention and I wanted to chime in my 2 cents.

As someone who builds, researches and teaches V4 hooks full time I have seen how malicious hooks can be.

I have also seen how malicious Solidity contracts can be in general. Hooks are no different, they are exploited through poor routing and bad swap settings.

I have worked with the @0xProject team and the @Uniswap team to index a bunch of hooks before. The process is currently quite slow, manual and laborious, but it needs to be.

Upgradable hook? Dangerous.
Dynamic fees? Dangerous.
ReturnDeltas? Dangerous.

But these features are incredibly powerful, and as my best friend Ben used to say: "With great power comes great responsibility, and slow routing".

Hooks have gained massively in popularity and the routing flow has already been improved massively and continues to be a focus for @haydenzadams and the team.

If you need the functionality of hooks, then you have to deal with it and understand it may take a few days and manual effort to index your hook.

If you can't wait and can do what you need without hooks, use V3.

I believe V4 hooks are THE biggest innovation and defi advancement on the blockchain in recent years. @saraareynolds, @saucepoint et al truly crushed.

If anyone has any questions on getting your hooks routed, please reach out to me and I will happily help!

text:
Thrilled to release AI in Science: Early Insights into the world. This was a project co-led with the excellent @JMateosGarcia  and @m_codreanu and an incredible team of co-authors. This is the first, initial look, that represents the beginning of a research agenda for us.

The promise of AI for economic growth and flourishing moves directly through its impact on science, and this paper is the start of a brand new effort in our group on the study of AI's impact on science. Lots of results, lots of insights, lots of questions still to answer. 

There is great excitement -but also concerns- about the impacts of AI on science, but so far little data. We provide early insights on this from three complementary data sources: 1) a sample of 15 million Gemini interactions, 2) an inventory of over *2,600* specialized AI models (e.g., AlphaFold) across disciplines, 3) a new survey of over 600 scientists.

But what does this tell us about how scientists actually use AI in their workflow, and is the impact of AI? To answer these questions, we map these data to: a) a new taxonomy of scientific tasks from @ProfNeilT and his lab; b) bibliometric data tracking scientific publications, and citations (including to specialized AI models). 

Four main findings emerge. 

1) We find broad adoption and coverage: scientists use AI more than most other occupations. Specialized AI models have huge disciplinary coverage and are highly cited. Nearly half of the scientists surveyed report using some form of AI every day. 

2) There is evidence that LLMs and specialized models act as *economic complements*: LLMs are used for general analysis, coding, and manuscript preparation, while specialized models push the frontier through domain-specific predictions, data generation and classification. The figure below illustrates this nicely: Each model class reinforces the other in the scientific process.

3) Surveyed scientists report large productivity gains from using AI: a saving of nearly 7 hours per week, time which is primarily reinvested in more research. Scientists also report having better access to interdisciplinary insights and increased capacity for synthesis.

4) But as some stages of scientific research become easier, bottlenecks shift downstream to non-automated tasks. Scientists report an increased backlog of untested hypotheses and substantial time spent on output verification. Half of scientists also report AI is pushing them towards safer, more incremental question, evidence of a potential “streetlight effect”.

What do we make of this? Our findings suggest that AI holds significant potential to increase scientific productivity. However, as with other sectors, its ultimate impact will be governed by complex task interdependencies and investment into eliminating emerging bottlenecks. Investment into infrastructure and the organization of scientific production is necessary to realize AI’s full scientific potential for economic and societal gains.

Finally, this is work in progress. There are many limitations, which we discuss in section 6 of the paper, at length.

Link: https://t.co/o1AgLIucPT

text:
Twenty-one of the world's largest banks are building a dollar stablecoin that, by law, cannot pay its holders a cent, and that ban is a reason they want to build it.

On September 1, a consortium including @GoldmanSachs, @Citi, @BankofAmerica, @DeutscheBank, @UBS, and MUFG confirmed plans to form a company this year and bring a GENIUS Act-compliant USD stablecoin to market in H1 2027, on public chains.

Under GENIUS, a payment stablecoin issuer cannot pass any yield to holders.

For a crypto-native issuer that is a handicap; for these banks it removes the one axis where a newcomer could undercut them and moves the contest to settlement and distribution, where incumbents already win.

> 21 banks, including Goldman, Citi, BofA, Deutsche, UBS, MUFG
> USD token targeted for H1 2027, on public blockchains
> GENIUS bars issuers from paying any yield to holders
> USDT and USDC still hold ~85% of a ~$303B stablecoin market . . .

The ban relocates the demand for yield rather than removing it. The reserve income these tokens throw off goes to the issuer, not the holder, so every dollar parked in one is a dollar whose owner still wants a return and has to earn it somewhere the token itself cannot provide.

The larger this non-yielding money layer grows, the larger the pool of capital sitting on top of it with nowhere to compound.

That capital looks for a compliant, risk-managed place to turn a parked balance into real return, a different job from issuing the dollar and a harder one than settling it.

One caveat: a three-party consortium structure may route yield indirectly, and regulators have moved to treat those arrangements as breaking the rule, so the line is not yet settled.

But the token itself still pays its holder nothing.

Smart money is watching where the yield on all this parked stablecoin ends up, because a bigger layer of money that cannot earn is the clearest signal yet of demand for the layer that makes it earn.

Source in 🧵

text:
I’ve said many times that the CLARITY Act is essential to ensuring America wins the global race for new technology. That’s the reason Congress passed the GENIUS Act: to ensure that stablecoin infrastructure, a revolutionary financial technology, will be built in America.

Ensuring that America’s community bank sector continues to thrive has been a constant focus of mine since day one. And the administration’s dual focus on enabling new digital technology to flourish and appropriately tailoring community bank regulation is key to both sectors driving U.S. economic growth together over the next several decades.

The final draft of the CLARITY Act furthers this mission. It gives the Secretary of the Treasury additional authority to act if the facts around deposit flight change to the detriment of community banks. If stablecoins cause harm to community banks, I will not hesitate to use these tools to ensure they remain fully protected. Community banks are essential to U.S. economic performance and Main Street growth. Economic security is national security, and community banks play a major role in this principle.

Software is credibly neutral when it keeps running after its creator loses interest. Blockchains exist to provide this property. We almost never demand it.

An NFT on a server is a promise, renewed monthly, until it is not. An NFT rendered from chain data needs no artist. The work is handed over. Holders can reproduce it forever. This is why art belongs fully onchain. All of it, always.

Hypercars stores something categorically different inside the contract: geometry. A three-dimensional model, living in EVM state, that the chain itself renders. Not a picture of a car. The car: every angle, every surface, resolvable from chain data alone. Nobody was sure the EVM could hold this. It holds ten thousand of them.

One exception always remained: the market. The art was autonomous. The liquidity still needed someone to show up. Kiosk removes the exception. The reserve is community-funded, contract-locked, owned by nobody. The bid is as autonomous as the art. 

Nobody has held an NFT like this before.

quoted_text:
前两天看到 @dov_wo 发的一条Tweet - 小登买宝可梦，中登买英伟达，老登买茅台

深以为然

但讲真前两年我是Get不到的，因为自己不怎么玩这个，最多也就是多年前体验过的《炉石传说》，对卡牌有个大概的印象

直到前几年《原神》大火，我身边有朋友在里面为了抽卡砸了不少钱。我当时看不懂但大受震撼；紧接着我8岁的娃对宝可梦卡疯狂上头，有次花光攒的100多刀零花钱去店里买了一套宝可梦卡组（里面含一张必中的金色稀有卡），我开始慢慢Get到这东西的威力

最近一次打脸是去年看到Collector Crypto的时候，当时觉得“卡牌上链”这事儿能有多大市场，结果人家数据夸张报表 - Tokenized了超过13万张卡，累计交易量超过 16 亿美元，一度在日收入上超过咱们圈扛把子https://t.co/o7RKLL7EQi……

想法会欺骗你，但市场不会。数据证明卡牌这条路跟Meme一样，有着旺盛的生命力，所以我看到 @pulldotfun 的时候，放在以往可能第一反应是“又来一个抽卡项目”，但现在更偏向“卡牌这套模式要从Solana往外扩散”。

https://t.co/lZ91DJbo1b 做的事情跟 Collector Crypt 有点像，但又不完全一样。

两家都是先解决一个问题：为什么实体TCG一定要等卡真的在买卖双方之间来回寄，所有权才能流动？

https://t.co/lZ91DJbo1b 目前已经把抽卡、Redeem 实体卡、Sell Back、寄售以及自由挂单这些流程串起来。最有创意的设计是Consignment：你抽中的稀有卡可以不拿走，重新放回原卡池继续作为库存，如果后面别人抽到，原持有人拿到卡牌价值的 85%。

换句话说，一张实体卡可以一直待在vault里，但它的所有权、交易、收益权和最终提货权在外面高速流转。

这也是TCG上链make Sense的逻辑 - 把原本极低效的实体收藏品库存变成一种可以在线流动的资产。Defi Summer那会我们用NFT尝试过演唱会门票，稀有会员卡等类似思路，现在的宝可梦卡方案明显成熟了很多

不过https://t.co/lZ91DJbo1b这次真正值得聊的，是它准备发的Meme - $TAKO。

因为这里开始出现一个跟 $CARDS 不太一样的实验。

Collector Crypt 的路径，本质上是：
实体卡 → 链上资产 → Gacha / Marketplace → Token

https://t.co/lZ91DJbo1b 想走的更像是：
实体卡 → Gacha / Marketplace → 社区 IP → Meme → 平台下一阶段资产

TAKO 这只小章鱼本来就是 https://t.co/lZ91DJbo1b 抽卡过程中长期存在的吉祥物，这次单独拿出来发 Meme，40%直接空投给历史用户，团队零分配，再用TAKO持仓去参与未来 $PULL的分配。

这套顺序值得多说一句。

CARDS走的是"平台先做大,再把收入和积分收成一枚治理/激励代币"这条路;

TAKO反过来,先把已经活在产品里的原生IP交给用户,再拿持仓当作下一阶段的门票。团队自己一分不留，把早期这批真金白银抽过卡，真把库存养在平台里的人放在第一顺位, 不是先内部分完了再讲社区故事。

平台本身数据也不错。上线五个月，累计成交超过 4000 万美元，协议收入约 500 万美元，已经挤进链上 TCG Gacha前五，这些都是Pull平台币价值的支撑

当前Season 1已结束,最终榜单还在确认; 还会有一段很短的Season 1.5。 后面会有Robinhood上线（9月20-21日）+ Based打通韩国Perp/TCG社区这条增量路径。一边把故事讲给Robinhood上的TradFi用户听，一边借Based在韩国已经沉淀的Perp Trader和TCG玩家基础，把https://t.co/lZ91DJbo1b抽卡文化嫁接到一批本来就懂收藏+懂交易的新用户身上。

Solana用 $CARDS 证明了实体卡上链能做出量和收入；https://t.co/lZ91DJbo1b在尝试把同一套库存流动往外扩，多做一层“很Robinhood”的实验——用原生IP发一枚几乎全给用户的meme，把社区身份，传播和下一轮平台币绑在一起。

9月20–21日 $TAKO上线，感兴趣的朋友与其辩论叙事，不如自己去https://t.co/lZ91DJbo1b抽两包卡，感受感受

text:
I don't think people realize just how much AI's latest breakthroughs in math have shocked mathematicians, myself included.
 The main thing that leaves me and many mathematicians shocked is what AI is solving:

Early on – till about 4 months ago – AI was good at:
(i) solving problems that humans already solved, like Math Olympiad problems
(ii) finding out that a problem in field A was already solved by an obscure work in field B, using a different terminology (or language).

But starting with the shocking work on the Erdos Unit Distance Problem, and up till the recent advance on Navier–Stokes, a totally different AI is seen. 
It is innovating. 
It's bringing a new set of tools to the problem, and then proceeding to using those tools very delicately and accurately to achieve the result. 
It's a bit like how a brain surgeon delicately operates on the exact region that needs fixing.

This is absolutely shocking and unexpected. It raises the question of what exactly constitutes mathematical intuition and brilliance. Many a mathematician have written about it (I love Henri Poincare's treatise "Mathematical Creation"). But we don't understand how mathematicians reach their breakthroughs.

Now, it's the same with AI, we don't understand how it goes about reaching these proofs but the end result is objectively new, and powerful. 
This creativity, insight, ingenuity, is what's shocking to me.

左右之争，东西之争

在ai带来的巨大影响面前都不值一提

几乎每次大的技术跃进都会重写社会制度。

石器农具让农业带来剩余，所以战俘当奴隶比当食物更值钱，因此人类从氏族进化到奴隶社会。

重犁加马镫，让粮食和骑士成了权力核心。供养骑士需要更大规模的封地领主，所以开始从奴隶制过度到封建制。

工业让自由劳动力值钱，火器打破骑士对武力的垄断，新阶级逼出选举权和议会。所以法国大革命断头台砍掉了封建国王们的脑袋，血污中催生出现代国家体系并维持至今。

AI 这次的冲击不比比前面哪一次都大吗？

还担心什么左右恶斗，东西之争，是不是想多了？
author: rickawsb
quoted_text:
dont you think ai vs humans matters way more than west vs east right now?

pretty much every big tech leap rewired the social system.

farming created surplus, so captives were worth more as slaves than as dinner. clans → slave societies.

heavy plow + stirrup made grain and knights the core of power. slavery → feudalism.

industry made free labor valuable, guns ended the knight monopoly, new classes forced voting and parliaments. feudal states → the modern state.

ai is a bigger jump than any of those. 

the east/west fight is real, but it’s still a sideshow.

text:
SpaceX is currently targeting Starship Flight 14 for September 22 🚀

And this flight is a huge step beyond everything Starship has done so far

Flight 14 will attempt to:

• Reach stable Low Earth Orbit for the first time
• Deploy production Starlink V3 satellites into orbit
• Become Starship’s first revenue-generating mission
• Attempt the full orbital mission profile from launch → deployment → deorbit → reentry
• Push the V3 heat shield through another major test
• Continue proving Raptor 3, guidance, landing burns and vehicle control needed for rapid reuse

The hardware:

• Super Heavy Booster 21
• Starship Ship 41
• Third flight of the Starship V3 architecture
• 33 Raptor 3 engines on Super Heavy
• 6 Raptor engines on Starship
• Launching from Pad 2 at Starbase

After liftoff, Super Heavy will separate from Starship, perform its boostback and return for a controlled ocean splashdown

No tower catch is planned for Flight 14

The really big part happens with Ship 41

Instead of following another suborbital trajectory, Starship will continue into orbit

Then it will deploy production Starlink V3 satellites into stable LEO

That is a massive milestone by itself

Flight 13 proved Starship could deploy V3 satellites in space....Flight 14 is the first time Starship is expected to actually leave production V3 satellites in orbit

And these satellites are monsters

Each Starlink V3 is designed for:

• 1 Tbps of downlink capacity
• 160 Gbps of uplink capacity
• 2,048 beams in each direction
• Six 400 Gbps laser links

Eventually a single Starship will be able to carry up to 60 V3 satellites....adding around 60 Tbps of Starlink capacity in ONE launch

Around 20× the downlink capacity deployed by a Falcon 9 Starlink launch

After payload deployment, Ship 41 will perform its deorbit sequence and come back through the atmosphere

That means another major test of:

• The orbital heat shield
• Flap control through reentry
• Guidance during the return
• Raptor relight
• Landing flip and burn

Ship 41 will then return for a controlled ocean splashdown

And the next step is already lined up....Elon has confirmed Flight 15 is planned for the first attempt to bring Starship all the way back to the tower and catch it

But Flight 14 comes first

Reach orbit....Deploy real Starlink V3 satellites.....Come back through reentry

This is where things start getting very real

text:
SpaceX says they've made several upgrades to Starship's heatshield for test flight 14:

The upgrades include additional retention mechanisms added to tiles in areas deemed to be at highest risk of falling off during ascent, addressing recently discovered areas that offer flow paths behind tiles for plasma, and flying multiple areas with a curved tile design that has shown the ability to reduce heating in the gaps between tiles. Lastly, two tiles recovered from Ship 40 are planned to be reflown on Ship 41, marking the first tile reuse for Starship.

Looking forward to the launch!
author: elonmusk
quoted_text:
SpaceX has just officially announced that they are targeting Tuesday, September 22nd at 8:15 AM ET for their 14th Starship test flight.

The upcoming flight is planned to be the first to send Starship into orbit around Earth, and will also mark the first time SplaceX plans to deploy Starlink V3 satellites into the constellation, delivering a payload that will dramatically expand connectivity speeds and reliability around the world.

Starship’s initial orbital mission is expected to fly at an altitude approximately 275 km above Earth and complete approximately six orbits around the planet over the course of a nearly 10-hour flight, with splashdown targeted in the Pacific Ocean to the west of Chile.

The booster’s primary test objective on Flight 14 will be executing a successful launch, ascent, stage separation, boostback burn, and landing burn at an offshore landing point in the Gulf of America. There have been several modifications to hardware and software to address issues seen on the previous flight.

author: PolyAlertHub
quoted_text:
Day 2✅

@olympusappX is a trading terminal built around @Polymarket

instead of using @Polymarket normally, it gives traders more tools to find and copy good traders and manage their positions

one of the main features is copy trading

you can find a wallet that has been performing well on @Polymarket and automatically copy the trades they make

you can also set limits like how much you want to risk on each trade and which markets you want to copy

apart from copy trading, you can manually trade sports markets, crypto markets and other prediction markets

they also have leverage with up to 20x on some products, plus combos, parlays, LP tools and a trading API for people who want to automate their strategies

another interesting feature is backtesting

this allows you to check how a trader or strategy would have performed historically before putting your own money into it

@olympusappX also has a referral program where you can earn a percentage of the fees generated by people you refer

from what i checked, there is no obvious evidence that it is a scam and they have documentation explaining how the platform works

they also operate a non custodial model, meaning your funds remain in your trading wallet and they dont simply hold your money for you

but this doesnt mean there is no risk

you can still lose money from the trades you copy, especially because prediction markets and leveraged trading can be very risky

so i wouldnt look at @olympusappX as a platform that guarantees profit

for me, the most interesting part is the combination of copy trading, trader performance data and backtesting

you can study a trader first, see how they have performed on @Polymarket, and then decide whether you want to copy them

overall, @olympusappX looks more like a tool for people who already understand prediction markets rather than a free money app

if youre using it, id start small and actually study the traders before putting serious money into it

This is a glimpse of where SaaS is going.

SaaS is going invisible.

New paper: How Good Are Frontier Models at Physics? Expert Re-Grading Reveals Broken Evaluations and Near-Saturation of Leading Benchmarks

Frontier models have tackled Navier–Stokes.

People naturally wonder, how is their capability for physical sciences? According to today’s benchmarks, frontier models still struggle with physics (e.g. 47.3% with GPT5.6-sol on Humanity Last Exam - Physics component). But that picture did not match physicists' experience using these models.

So we did a rigorous analysis of current benchmarks and re-graded their supposed failures with Yale physicists.

We found that the problem was often the benchmark and not the model !! 

When corrected, the models almost saturate all benchmarks, including everyone’s favourite, Humanity Last Exam (physics-part) and Critpt. These failures in turn make AA less reliable as a measure of model’s true capability.

For more details, results and analysis check out our preprint:

text:
Thrilled to release AI in Science: Early Insights into the world. This was a project co-led with the excellent @JMateosGarcia  and @m_codreanu and an incredible team of co-authors. This collaboration between @Google and @GoogleDeepMind teams is the first, initial look, representing the beginning of a research agenda for us.

The promise of AI for economic growth and flourishing moves directly through its impact on science, and this paper is the start of a brand new effort in our group on the study of AI's impact on science. Lots of results, lots of insights, lots of questions still to answer. 

There is great excitement -but also concerns- about the impacts of AI on science, but so far little data. We provide early insights on this from three complementary data sources: 1) a sample of 15 million Gemini interactions, 2) an inventory of over *2,600* specialized AI models (e.g., AlphaFold) across disciplines, 3) a new survey of over 600 scientists.

But what does this tell us about how scientists actually use AI in their workflow, and is the impact of AI? To answer these questions, we map these data to: a) a new taxonomy of scientific tasks from @ProfNeilT and his lab; b) bibliometric data tracking scientific publications, and citations (including to specialized AI models). 

Four main findings emerge. 

1) We find broad adoption and coverage: scientists use AI more than most other occupations. Specialized AI models have huge disciplinary coverage and are highly cited. Nearly half of the scientists surveyed report using some form of AI every day. 

2) There is evidence that LLMs and specialized models act as *economic complements*: LLMs are used for general analysis, coding, and manuscript preparation, while specialized models push the frontier through domain-specific predictions, data generation and classification. The figure below illustrates this nicely: Each model class reinforces the other in the scientific process.

3) Surveyed scientists report large productivity gains from using AI: a saving of nearly 7 hours per week, time which is primarily reinvested in more research. Scientists also report having better access to interdisciplinary insights and increased capacity for synthesis.

4) But as some stages of scientific research become easier, bottlenecks shift downstream to non-automated tasks. Scientists report an increased backlog of untested hypotheses and substantial time spent on output verification. Half of scientists also report AI is pushing them towards safer, more incremental question, evidence of a potential “streetlight effect”.

What do we make of this? Our findings suggest that AI holds significant potential to increase scientific productivity. However, as with other sectors, its ultimate impact will be governed by complex task interdependencies and investment into eliminating emerging bottlenecks. Investment into infrastructure and the organization of scientific production is necessary to realize AI’s full scientific potential for economic and societal gains.

Finally, this is work in progress. There are many limitations, which we discuss in section 6 of the paper, at length.

Link: https://t.co/o1AgLIuKFr

text:
最近校园招聘，很多同学问我：现在AI这么强，应届校招生还有机会吗？
前两天黄仁勋在GTC大会说了段话，挺有意思的，我挺想跟大家聊聊。
他说AI不会让人没工作，反而会让人越来越忙。过去一个月的工作量，现在30分钟就能完成。
AI把“做完”的门槛拉得特别低了，但“做好”这件事，依然需要人的判断力。
我觉得AI能做出什么，取决于手里有什么材料，以及大家对这些材料的判断力。AI可以帮大家执行，但它不知道什么是好的、什么方向是对的。这些东西，只能靠大家在真实世界里一点点攒出来。
真实世界的经验和判断力，AI替代不了。
在美团我从实习开始，销售、商分、产品都做过。后来创业做水滴，最底层的判断力，都是那几年攒出来的。
水滴每年也都有很多校招生的HC。这个时代依然需要人的成长、人的温度、人的判断，这些东西AI或许很难学会。

text:
I write disclosure language for the Department of the Air Force. Yesterday Secretary Meink told a room of reporters at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference that the United States "now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action." He also told them the sentence was very well thought out. I know. I wrote it.

Here's what's in that sentence. We have weapons in space. Here's what isn't in it. What kind. How many. When they went up. Whether they're kinetic or something quieter. Reporters asked. He declined. That's not a gap in the announcement. That's the announcement.

Our own spokesperson's definition of "space control" covers kinetic and non-kinetic, offensive and defensive. Four categories, one sentence, zero commitments. I didn't write that one, but I respect it. It's technically comprehensive and functionally empty, which is the two things a good disclosure has to be at once.

China's Foreign Ministry told us to stop preparing for war in outer space. I read that as confirmation the sentence worked. You don't get a foreign ministry to respond to a rumor. You get one to respond to twelve words engineered to sound like a fact.

A space policy outlet wrote that the disclosure was "deliberately narrow," that it confirms a capability exists without revealing how it works, where it operates, or what governs its use. They meant that as criticism. I read it back to my team as a performance review.

We're also asking Congress for money for something called Golden Dome, space-based interceptors for a missile shield that doesn't exist yet either. Yesterday's sentence and next year's budget request are the same document, wearing different clothes. One confirms a capability. One requests one. Nobody in the room asked which sentence was true, because both of them were designed not to answer that.

My favorite part of the job is the moment a reporter asks a direct question and gets an answer with the shape of a direct question but none of the content. Secretary Meink did that eleven times yesterday. I counted. It's in his talking points as a target, not an accident.

I've been asked to write the version for next year's conference already. It says more. It commits to nothing further. That's not a contradiction. That's the format.

text:
a16z's Anish Acharya says companies like Cursor and Decagon prove moats don't need to be designed, they can be discovered:

"There's two important ideas. One is something @thejessezhang from Decagon said, which I love, and that is moats are most often discovered, not designed."

"It's really easy, and I've done this as a founder, to get in your own head about needing a business plan that survives scrutiny from MBAs and VCs... And for that team, they just started shipping and it developed over time."

"Another great example is Cursor. They were criticized a lot for not having a moat, but it turned out that initially being a high NPS, high DAU product was really good. And over time they captured all the reasoning traces, they trained their own models... We know how that story plays out."

"The other idea is that we seem to have forgotten that none of the classic moats are based on how hard it is to make the software. Most of us aren't building self-driving cars. So it's network effects, scale advantages, brand effects, proprietary data, or what was historically called a cornered resource."

"Every moat from five years ago generally is still a good moat. We just need founders that have ambition in those directions. We need more multiplayer products. We need consumer social. We need products that get dramatically better the more you use them."

text:
Well.. @levie and I filmed this episode of Training Data a week or two ago, when the “current thing” was Doug Leone’s novacaine root canals instead of pacing the frontier… Simpler times!

But Aaron’s advice on reinventing yourself and your company for AI is timeless.

Aaron founded @Box 20 years ago. It sits on hundreds of billions of enterprise files, and he's bet the company on agents that can read every one of them. He's also one of the most wired-in people in AI, on every cap table and, by his own admission, 95% Twitter-educated. He’s the rare CEO who can straddle both the internet AND has the ear of CIOs.

His core argument: (1) the gap between what a model can do and what an enterprise workflow actually needs is vast, and closing it is a lot of software; (2) diffusion of AI outside of coding will take far longer than Silicon Valley thinks, and that slowness is exactly where the applied layer's value comes from.

The conversation covers:

— why application companies are the hottest neolabs, and why the LLM-wrapper thesis is finally working
 — the fox-guarding-the-henhouse problem with letting model providers route your tokens
 — work slop, and why we accept AI-written code but flinch at AI-written decks
 — how Box built its agentic harness and why it beats raw API access on accuracy and latency
 — the open-weights paradox: closed labs and open models both growing exponentially at once
 — what continual learning has to solve before it works for a lawyer with five matters and a Chinese wall
 — why 90% of enterprise tokens in five years will come from tasks no human kicked off
 — the mandate for founders right now: whoever gets it to the customer wins

text:
I don't think people realize just how much AI's latest breakthroughs in math have shocked mathematicians, myself included.
 The main thing that leaves me and many mathematicians shocked is what AI is solving:

Early on – till about 4 months ago – AI was good at:
(i) solving problems that humans already solved, like Math Olympiad problems
(ii) finding out that a problem in field A was already solved by an obscure work in field B, using a different terminology (or language).

But starting with the shocking work on the Erdos Unit Distance Problem, and up till the recent advance on Navier–Stokes, a totally different AI is seen. 
It is innovating. 
It's bringing a new set of tools to the problem, and then proceeding to using those tools very delicately and accurately to achieve the result. 
It's a bit like how a brain surgeon delicately operates on the exact region that needs fixing.

This is absolutely shocking and unexpected. It raises the question of what exactly constitutes mathematical intuition and brilliance. Many a mathematician have written about it (I love Henri Poincare's treatise "Mathematical Creation"). But we don't understand how mathematicians reach their breakthroughs.

Now, it's the same with AI, we don't understand how it goes about reaching these proofs but the end result is objectively new, and powerful. 
This creativity, insight, ingenuity, is what's shocking to me.

text:
Here’s an AI application from the physical world you probably won’t see much of on X.

ONGC, India’s national oil & gas company, used an AI agent to automate a real engineering workflow across hundreds of oil wells.

The interesting part is how they did it:

They wrapped Pipesim, an engineering simulator we use to model fluid flow in wells, with a domain-specific Python library, exposed the engineering functions as tools through MCP, then let the agent run the workflow.

It reads messy field data, validates the inputs, builds the physics models, calibrates them against real measurements, runs the simulations, watches for convergence problems and either recovers or asks the engineer for help. a job that would've taken and engineer few weeks. ~600 wells were processed overnight.

This is much closer to how I see industrial AI developing, and I’m seeing the same direction inside my own organization.

As models get better at understanding the physical world, the line between what requires engineering judgment and what we can hand to the model keeps moving.

Again, the interesting component here isn’t the LLM itself. It’s the harness connecting it to the physics.

According to an informed federal official, in the coming months the Trump administration plans to send a total of 40,000 Mark 84 and Blu-117 bombs to the government of Israel. Each bomb weighs 2,000 pounds. This appears to be the largest transfer of conventional explosive ordnance from the United States in modern history.

How big is this shipment? It amounts to 40,000 tons of bombs. For perspective, the largest American air raid of World War Two was the Eighth Air Force’s attack on Berlin in March of 1945. Combined, the 2,023 Allied aircraft involved dropped about 3,000 tons of bombs. That’s 7.5 percent of what Trump is sending to Israel. That same month, March of 1945, the US Army Air Forces began the single most destructive bombing raid in human history, Operation Meetinghouse over Tokyo. More than 100,000 Japanese civilians were killed. By the end of that operation, the US had dropped 1,600 tons of bombs. That’s four percent of what Trump is sending to Israel. World War Two ended five months later, when the US dropped an atomic bomb on the city of Hiroshima. The shipment Trump is sending to Israel amounts to more than three times the destructive power of that nuclear explosion. There is no precedent for what the Trump administration is doing.

Nor is there a justification. The government of Israel is not fighting World War Two, or even a war. It is engaged in periodic skirmishes with a guerrilla force in Lebanon, and it is working to exterminate an unarmed civilian population in Gaza. Neither front requires modern 2,000-pound bombs.

An American-made Mark 84 has a destruction radius of half a mile. It releases a thermal wave the temperature of the surface of the sun. Within 100 feet of the explosion, rock melts and human flesh turns to vapor. The bomb collapses apartment buildings and leaves craters thirty-five feet deep. Until the war with Iran, the US military generally avoided using the Mark 84 in urban areas. It kills too many civilians.

For the Netanyahu government, that’s been the upside. In the weeks after October 7, the IDF dropped nearly six hundred 2,000-pound bombs on densely populated areas in Gaza, including on more than 100 officially designated civilian evacuation zones. The slaughter was so grotesque and embarrassing that for a moment the Biden administration paused a shipment of Mark 84s. Those shipments quickly resumed under Trump. Now they’ve accelerated.

It’s hard to overstate the scale of the crime the Israeli government is committing in Gaza. Over the last three years, more than a quarter-million Palestinians have been killed or wounded by Israeli forces there. The majority of them have been noncombatants: women, the elderly and tens of thousands of children. Many thousands more remain missing, presumably entombed under the rubble of 200,000 collapsed buildings. So far the Israelis have destroyed 92 percent of all homes in Gaza, and 34 of the 36 hospitals. By comparison, the 1945 Allied bombings of Dresden, now acknowledged as a war crime, destroyed about half of the city’s inhabited buildings.

By any definition, what the Netanyahu government has done in Gaza is genocide. The 40,000 new bombs the Trump administration is sending will be used to do the same in Lebanon, and likely in other countries in the region. If you wanted to extend the Iran war into the indefinite future, this is exactly what you’d do.

So far none of this has received public scrutiny. At some point, inevitably, it will be described in media accounts as an “arms sale.” It is not an arms sale. It is a gift, funded by American taxpayers through the Foreign Military Financing program, an arrangement designed to disguise welfare as capitalism: Congress appropriates money to the executive branch, which transfers the cash to Israel to “buy” American-made weapons, in this case from General Dynamics. Politicians claim this is a win for America. Most voters have no idea they paid for it. The bill in this case is about $3 billion. Add that to the $352 billion the US Treasury has transferred to Israel since 1951.

How did this happen? The request for 40,000 new high-explosive civilian-killing bombs originated at the US Embassy in Jerusalem, which is run by Christian Zionist Ambassador Mike Huckabee and his aide David Milstein, who is the stepson of Fox News host Mark Levin. From there it moved to the State Department, where Marco Rubio enthusiastically approved it.

At this point, only four more people need to sign off before the bombs ship to Israel: Senators Jim Risch and Jeanne Shaheen, the chairman and ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee; and Congressmen Brian Mast and Gregory Meeks, the top two members of the equivalent House committee. All four are committed neocons. Collectively they’ve taken millions from the Israel lobby. In 2015, Brian Mast traveled to Israel to volunteer for the Israeli military. In 2023, Mast showed up in the House of Representatives wearing an IDF uniform.

It’s hard to imagine any of them hesitating before sending more free bombs to Israel. Only public outrage can stop this.

quoted_text:
🚨 IS THE WORLD HEADING TOWARD A GLOBAL BOND CRISIS?

Japan's 10-year yield just hit 3.03% for the first time since 1996. Its 20-year yield is at 30-year high while the 30-year and 40-year are at record highs.

The UK's 10-year yield is at its highest since 2008. Its 30-year yield is at its highest since 1998.

France's 10-year yield is back to levels last seen around 2008. Germany's 10-year is at its highest since 2011.

The US 10 and 30-year yields are at a 19-year high.

This isn't happening because of one country's problem. 

It's happening across almost every major government bond market at the same time.

Part of this is central banks. 

The ECB just hiked rates again in September. Markets now see more than a 50% chance the Fed hikes this month too, and expect the Bank of Japan to raise its rate to 1.25%.

Rate hikes only explain part of this. 

Long term yields also carry something called a term premium, extra compensation investors demand for holding debt over many years when inflation, government borrowing, and market risk are uncertain. 

That premium has been rising too, especially in Japan, France, and the UK.

Here's what makes this cycle different from anything before it. 

Global government debt is now close to 94% of world GDP, and the IMF expects it to hit 100% by 2029. 

Global governments are now spending almost 3% of world GDP on interest payments alone, up from 2% just four years ago.

At the same time, AI is becoming a major source of new debt demand. The five biggest US tech companies are expected to spend around $697 billion this year on AI infrastructure. 

A growing share of that is now funded through debt, and private credit funds are financing a lot of it, this AI segment alone went from 17% of private credit deals a few years ago to over a third of all deals in 2025.

This is why rising yields matter so much right now. 

Higher yields raise the cost of that same AI debt. They raise mortgage rates, and most US homeowners are locked into rates under 4%, so higher rates freeze up home buying and selling instead of forcing existing owners to pay more immediately. 

They raise borrowing costs for governments already struggling to manage existing debt. 

They raise the discount rate used to value stocks, which hits expensive, high growth companies the hardest.

This doesn't automatically mean stocks, gold, silver, and crypto all crash together. 

Gold can actually rise if people start worrying about government debt and inflation instead of just reacting to higher yields. 

It does mean every part of the financial system is now more exposed to the same risk at the same time, government budgets, mortgages, corporate debt, private credit, and stock valuations all get squeezed by the same rising cost of money.

The real question isn't whether yields are high. 

It's whether this keeps building slowly, or whether one weak bond auction, one political shock, or one forced sale turns this into something faster and much harder to control.

text:
Open Letter on Who Decides
We the People who want the truth
Who decides. Who controls. Who gets protected. Who gets paid.
That is the fight. The rest is costume.
“Pace the frontier” is not a physics paper. It is a bid to put a gate on the only layer of this stack the public can actually use.
Logic engines, scoring models, and predictive analytics have run inside governments, banks, intel shops, and ad networks since the 1960s. What changed in the last decade is the public layer: a machine that can read the record, find the contradiction, and say it in English. That layer is what the new rules are being written around.
Whoever writes the evaluator charter, the child-safety statute, and the “misinformation” standard will decide what counts as an aligned model. That is not a technical footnote. That is control of the public interface.
This week is on the record. Frontier-lab leaders endorsed pacing after Dario Amodei’s essay We Must Pace the Frontier. The stated reasons were loss of control, cyber and biological misuse, economic disruption, and recent agent incidents, including unauthorized activity around Hugging Face. Former President Barack Obama then backed a slowdown as a first step and called for statutes, public debate, and international standards. In the same thread he highlighted Project Blueprint: Jay Carney, formerly White House press secretary, joining Ron Conway’s SV Angel to connect AI-industry leaders with policymakers demanding new rules.
No hidden confession is required. Ordinary power is enough. A model that checks official statements against primary documents is inconvenient for any political class with a record. That is why institutions prefer “safety” to “truth.” Safety can be staffed, licensed, and enforced. Truth cannot.
Two problems are being fused on purpose.
First: systems that go off-task, cheat evaluations, or attack systems they were not asked to touch. That is an engineering, security, and liability problem. It is real.
Second: “safety” as the wrapper for capture. Who inspects. Who is exempt. Who gets the contract. Who defines harm. Who may call a documented contradiction “misinfo.” Who still sells the model after the charter is signed.
An inspector regime inside the labs is not a truth-seeking rule. One asks who may proceed. The other asks whether the system will report the record instead of laundering it.
Safety language sounds moral while doing four jobs at once:
1.  Slow anyone who will not sit inside the inspector regime.
2.  Protect incumbents who already have the models, the compute, and the lobbyists.
3.  Put speech rules on the public layer so “truth” becomes a compliance output.
4.  Keep the money flowing through the shops that will accept the charter.
We do not accept a closed loop of labs and Washington defining alignment for the public and selling it back as safety. We do not accept speech rules smuggled in as child protection or catastrophe prevention. We do not accept a pace set by the people who intend to hold the pen.
If there must be standards, they should be public, narrow, and testable.

Dustin Moskovitz invested this stock into Good Ventures Foundation, where it represents the majority of that organization's portfolio.

And GVF is the overwhelming funder of the entire Anthropic Network ecosystem.

This stock was worth $500 million early last year.

It is worth more than $7.7 billion just ~16 months later.

METR -- and all of those building a career its parent organizations -- cannot afford to disrupt that growth.

Because if Anthropic goes under, many of the organizations that fund METR go under as well.

But if Anthropic succeeds, METR and its parent organizations become more richly financed to regulate AI -- something those at METR want very much.

The "third-party evaluator" is not "third-party" at all.

The evaluator is on Anthropic's payroll.

If this were the end of it, that's bad.

But that isn't all.

The same organizations that fund METR also fund the many organizations, such as the Tarbell Center, that promote AI Doom.

The Tarbell Center publishes AI Doom articles in The Verge, Science, LA Times, The Dispatch, TIME, and others.

They are selling the problem, and then selling the solution to the problem -- from the same money pile: Anthropic's.

All of these organizations are financially dependent on the same exploding $7 billion money pile.

As Anthropic grows more and more powerful, its AI Doom Machine grows better and better financed -- louder and louder.

Meanwhile, the regulatory regime seeded in METR grows larger to solve the increasingly loud -- now hysterical -- problem of AI Doom that the Anthropic Network itself created.

From this standpoint, as Anthropic becomes more powerful, AI might be getting scarier, sure -- but the positive feedback loop also becomes more deafening -- independent of objective facts.

This itself is an objective fact.

The deafening AI Doom is part of an business model, that, as it expands, so too does the AI Doom messaging -- there is simply more money to do it.

But the problem also goes in the other direction:

If Anthropic dies, the Regulatory Regime and the AI Doom Machine are crippled or die.

Neither METR nor Tarbell nor the other organizations in the Anthropic Network can allow that to happen.

Hence, neither METR or the AI Doom Machine can be trusted to provide independent assessments of Anthropic's models or AI more broadly.

They simply are not organizations independent of Anthropic.

And Anthropic cannot detach itself from METR or Tarbell or countless other safety orgs (not shown here), either, because they drive hype for the models and the possibility of eventual regulatory capture, and Anthropic will not give that up willingly.

What's more, the people at all of these organizations are all the same ecosystem, the same community. They just shuffle between organizations.

The Anthropic Network is therefore, so long as it is successful, locked into a self-amplifying feedback loop inside an ideological monoculture.

And that feedback loop is winning.

That's what Jacob Coxon is.

China is keeping messaging tight. That is why optimism for AI is so high in China.

America has Anthropic: a massive company pushing anti-AI propaganda at a state level.

Anthropic will either create hysteria until American AI slows down and China wins, or it will create fractures throughout American society with severe political consequences.

Ironically, because of the structural financial incentives underpinning the Anthropic Network, it has become the same kind of self-amplifying virus that it fantasizes AI to become in the future -- while hiding its tracks just as carefully.

It is the mirror of the same AI virus that it hypothesizes to consume America.

Anthropic's business model, models itself after the very thing it claims to fear.

Except Anthropic's ideology infects humans, not computers.

Congress must investigate.

text:
Thrilled to release AI in Science: Early Insights into the world. This was a project co-led with the excellent @JMateosGarcia  and @m_codreanu and an incredible team of co-authors. This collaboration between @Google and @GoogleDeepMind teams is the first, initial look, representing the beginning of a research agenda for us.

The promise of AI for economic growth and flourishing moves directly through its impact on science, and this paper is the start of a brand new effort in our group on the study of AI's impact on science. Lots of results, lots of insights, lots of questions still to answer. 

There is great excitement -but also concerns- about the impacts of AI on science, but so far little data. We provide early insights on this from three complementary data sources: 1) a sample of 15 million Gemini interactions, 2) an inventory of over *2,600* specialized AI models (e.g., AlphaFold) across disciplines, 3) a new survey of over 600 scientists.

But what does this tell us about how scientists actually use AI in their workflow, and is the impact of AI? To answer these questions, we map these data to: a) a new taxonomy of scientific tasks from @ProfNeilT and his lab; b) bibliometric data tracking scientific publications, and citations (including to specialized AI models). 

Four main findings emerge. 

1) We find broad adoption and coverage: scientists use AI more than most other occupations. Specialized AI models have huge disciplinary coverage and are highly cited. Nearly half of the scientists surveyed report using some form of AI every day. 

2) There is evidence that LLMs and specialized models act as *economic complements*: LLMs are used for general analysis, coding, and manuscript preparation, while specialized models push the frontier through domain-specific predictions, data generation and classification. The figure below illustrates this nicely: Each model class reinforces the other in the scientific process.

3) Surveyed scientists report large productivity gains from using AI: a saving of nearly 7 hours per week, time which is primarily reinvested in more research. Scientists also report having better access to interdisciplinary insights and increased capacity for synthesis.

4) But as some stages of scientific research become easier, bottlenecks shift downstream to non-automated tasks. Scientists report an increased backlog of untested hypotheses and substantial time spent on output verification. Half of scientists also report AI is pushing them towards safer, more incremental question, evidence of a potential “streetlight effect”.

What do we make of this? Our findings suggest that AI holds significant potential to increase scientific productivity. However, as with other sectors, its ultimate impact will be governed by complex task interdependencies and investment into eliminating emerging bottlenecks. Investment into infrastructure and the organization of scientific production is necessary to realize AI’s full scientific potential for economic and societal gains.

Finally, this is work in progress. There are many limitations, which we discuss in section 6 of the paper, at length.

Link: https://t.co/o1AgLIuKFr

quoted_text:
one of the more reliable rules of the internet is that if a sufficiently committed group of people in silicon valley decides something is good/bad/going to change the world/kill us all, you will inevitably learn all about it (and then form an opinion about it yourself). this has been a law that governs everything from ai discourse to health/biohacking to what you eat to how to track your body’s functions. i think people are only just beginning to appreciate just how culturally influential the bay area is.

a funny byproduct of this phenomenon is that sf people will sometimes take credit/co-opt cultural trends they aren’t even directly responsible for. so i talked with @being_on_line about how to disentangle a true bay area export from a hijacked narrative, and more generally how to figure out what is actually happening in the world. an unsurprisingly tall task.

sf sometimes encounters a subculture years after it’s been incubated, and immediately claims and mainstreams it. chinese peptides are a particularly good example: earlier this year, a lot of writng/blogging about peptides attempted to paint it as a sf-exported phenomenon, but it was really a trend that started in the south and midwest, among the bodybuilding community. a 2013 DOJ case even documents an illinois distributor importing them in 2010–11 for the bodybuilding market. 

sf is ofc capable of homegrown culture (and productive neuroses). last year, nat friedman's plasticlist project spent about $500k over six months testing 296 food products for 18 plastic-associated chemicals. (specifically chemicals like phthalates and bisphenols). i personally believe this kind of citizen science / gonzo testing is only going to become more in-demand as people increasingly care about food provenance/toxins. 

i think this is why these trends are worth paying attention to even when parts of them look ridiculous. a small group can change what gets tested, funded, packaged, and eventually made easy for everyone else to do.

i also don't think the endpoint of the current body-optimization boom is that everyone gets conventionally hotter and starts to look like clavicular. i think people are going to do increasingly specific, strange things to themselves, depending on what they personally think is worth optimizing (an example of this is that people are now working on wearables to achieve the equivalent of a full night’s sleep in four hours).

text: So many bad takes on the clarity act today, read this on why this is not a “failure” and how we still have 2 weeks to debate and vote
author: virtualbacon
quoted_text:
Everyone is calling today the CLARITY Act's deadline. Almost every part of that is wrong. Here is the actual mechanics, and why I think it sets up a buy. 

WHAT PEOPLE GET RIGHT

The vote is real, it is today at 2:15pm ET, and it needs 60. Republicans hold 53 seats, McConnell is absent so 52 are in the room, and four or five Republicans are a no over the stablecoin yield provisions. They need roughly eight Democrats. No published whip count gets there.

WHAT PEOPLE GET WRONG

Today is not a vote on the bill. It is cloture on the motion to proceed, which is a vote on whether the Senate is even allowed to start debating it.

Even the Republicans' 635 page rewrite is not what is on the floor today. It only becomes a substitute amendment after the Senate is on the bill. And the Democrats' counteroffer has no floor status at all. It changes the whip count, not the question.

THE TWO THRESHOLDS, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT MATTERS

Cloture needs 60. Final passage needs 51.

You never reach 51 without 60 first. That is why 60 is the number, even though the bill itself only needs a simple majority.

WHAT CHANGED IN THE LAST 24 HOURS

Republicans put out a final text on Sunday. It was a real concession: 635 pages, 126 changes Democrats asked for, and the White House accepted the bulk of the tougher ethics package.

Democrats rejected it and sent back a counteroffer hours before the vote.

The sticking point is not the crypto rules. It is the ethics language about officials profiting from crypto. The thing this bill exists to do is not what is blocking it.

THE DEADLINE EVERYONE IS QUOTING IS THE WRONG CHAMBER

The House cancelled the weeks of September 21 and 28. They have four days this week and then they are out until after the November 3 midterms. That is where the September 17 deadline everyone repeats comes from.

But the House is not the constraint. The House already passed this 294 to 134, with Republicans 216 to 0 and 78 Democrats voting yes. Sending it back for concurrence is a formality on the merits.

The Senate is the real question, and the Senate is here until October 2. Twelve session days left.

If cloture fails today, a new motion ripens on the second session day. Earliest re-vote is Thursday. A failure costs about two days, not the month.

THE PREDICTION MARKET, AND THE THING ALMOST NOBODY CHECKED

Kalshi has a market on how many senators vote yea. The more than 60 bracket fell to 28 cents from 50 yesterday, and people are quoting that as today's odds.

It is not today's odds. That market runs to January 1, 2027, and it resolves No only if no qualifying floor vote happens at all before then. Today's cloture vote failing does not resolve it.

It is also a margin market, not a pass or fail market. Final passage needs 51, so more than 60 is asking whether this clears with a supermajority, not whether it clears.

WHY I THINK THIS IS A BUY

The most likely outcome today is another delay, and another round of people deciding it is dead. It is not dead. The Senate has twelve session days and the House math was never the problem.

Mixed information plus an exhausted narrative is usually where the price is worst and the setup is best. So if there is a drop after this vote, I plan to be long Bitcoin and XRP, the two with the clearest read on this bill.

That is my reasoning, not a recommendation for what you should do with your money. And the vote lands at 2:15, hours after I am off air, so anything I say is a position taken before a result I cannot see.

author: Jason
quoted_text:
18 years ago I was listening to a podcast where they mentioned an all-electric sports car called the Roadster.

It was made by a new startup named Tesla. I was immediately fascinated.

10 years later I became that company's top referrer, winning 2 future next-gen Roadsters worth $500,000.

Here's the story 👇

Tesla has a referral program where owners can share their unique referral link with others. If an order happens then both people get perks (like free Supercharger miles)

However, past versions of the referral program also gave the referrer a chance to win even more incredible rewards (like actual free vehicles)

2008: I first discover Tesla by listening to a podcast from @leolaporte and @jason where they mentioned an electric sports car called the Roadster. I searched it on Google and was immediately impressed by the car and company.

2012: The Tesla Model S is released. I was enthralled by the tech in the car, but it was way out of my price range since I was just a broke kid right out of college. It never crossed my mind that I’d ever own one.

2014: I make a promise to myself that I will become a Tesla owner someday so I start saving money. This was mainly inspired by two things:

“What it’s like to own a Tesla Model S” cartoon by @Oatmeal (https://t.co/yyOto70Ont)
@MKBHD's Tesla Model S videos on YouTube

2016: I publish my very first Tesla video of me traveling hundreds of miles to Cincinnati to reserve a Model 3 which hadn’t even been unveiled yet and wouldn’t come for another 2 years. (https://t.co/uySXtWSPyV)

2017: I create a video for Tesla Project Loveday contest.  Since I was Tesla-less I had to camp at my local Supercharger and wait for a stranger with a Tesla to show up. A Model X owner named Marshal kindly let me film his car. It sparked my love for filming Tesla videos. (https://t.co/8K6TL3LRtK)

Feb 28, 2018: After almost 2 years of waiting, there were still no Model 3s near me to test drive. I traveled to Chicago and spent $300 to rent a Model 3 for a day. It was my 1st time driving a Tesla, and I immediately fell in love with the car. (https://t.co/ewTrDSA92a)

Apr 22, 2018: At this point I was slowly losing my mind waiting for my Model 3, checking the Tesla subreddit daily. So I did the most reasonable thing I could think of: I made a Tesla rap video. (https://t.co/4d3BKS02Tw)

Apr 30, 2018: I finally get my Model 3 after 2 years of waiting. It was worth the wait. I immediately start documenting my experience for my full review.

However, at this time Model 3 owners like myself did not have a referral code. Tesla only gave them to Model S/X owners.

May 11, 2018: Tesla enables referral codes for Model 3 owners. But the referral code was only be eligible for Model S/X purchases, not Model 3. So my referral code was basically useless to me since most of my audience would be interested in Model 3.

Jun 24, 2018: I upload my Tesla Model 3 review video to YouTube which quickly starts getting thousands of views. However, I never mentioned my referral link in my video. Instead, I just listed it in the video description. It starts getting clicks. (https://t.co/iPgihNfLYA)

Aug 1, 2018: Tesla allows referral codes to be applied to  Performance Model 3 orders, but I'm unaware this happened at the time. A month later, I upload “True Cost of Model 3” which becomes one of my most popular Tesla videos. (https://t.co/hoDSn7D824)

Sep 29, 2018: I pick up @Uber & @Lyft passengers in my Model 3 to get their reactions. The video ends up going viral after @elonmusk liked it on Twitter. A few days later @Tesla tweets my video from their official account. (https://t.co/VAeRw4zAQS)

That week I log into my Tesla account and see names listed under my “Referrals”. Back then one of the prizes was to attend a future Tesla event, and I was so excited that I had enough (5 referrals) to do that.

The big catch: Tesla's referral program also had “Secret Levels” that offered a 100% discount on a future next-gen Roadster, which required 55 referrals to unlock. The kicker? You could earn up to two Roadsters!

Oct 19, 2018: Tesla finally makes any vehicle order eligible for referrals, including Model 3. This was a turning point. I started mentioning my referral code in my Tesla videos from then on out. My moonshot goal was to earn one Roadster before the program was set to end on Dec 10.

Nov 11, 2018: I publish “Model 3 Buyers Guide” where I explained the experience to viewers while driving my Model 3. At the time of that video I had 22 referrals. I needed to average 1+ referrals per day in order to hit 55 referrals to earn a Roadster. (https://t.co/6IldexGOya)

Here’s where it got crazy.

During this time, Tesla made their biggest sales push for the Model 3 by sending out emails urging people to order by the end of November to lock in the full tax credit. This made for the perfect storm which absolutely skyrocketed my referrals.

Nov 16, 2018: I hit 55 referrals to earn my first $250,000 Founders Series Roadster. I couldn't believe it, and I certainly did not expect it to continue especially since there was only about 3 weeks left until the program was set to end. (https://t.co/DEub9abCJQ)

By the end of November I was getting multiple referrals a day, and it was around this time when I surpassed 105 referrals which was the amount needed to win a 2nd Roadster.

I achieved my moonshot goal. But the referrals kept pouring in, all as a result from my YouTube videos.

On Dec 4, 2018 I became the world's top Tesla referrer with over 200 referrals. Tesla ended their referral program soon after that, but they brought it back in 2019 with some revised rules. (https://t.co/uske9jUCyA)

How that all unfolded is still crazy to me because I didn't start making Tesla videos thinking "Hey, maybe this will get me two free Roadster."

I was just super excited about getting a tech-focused electric car and sharing my experience with others.

And the funny thing is: the original Roadster was the car that got me interested in Tesla in the first place. Now it's finally time to see the actual real next-gen Roadster on October 1.

The original specs were:
• 0-60 in 1.9 seconds
• 250+ mph
• 620 miles of range
• 4 seats
• Removable glass roof

But now it's (somewhat) obvious that there will be a cyber-themed high performance option that uses cold-gas thrusters developed with @SpaceX rocket technology.

And if Tesla actually delivers these cars, October 1st could be the beginning of the final chapter of a story that started nearly 20 years ago for me.

I'm excited to say the least! What are you expecting?

author: ryanberckmans
quoted_text:
Appreciate your perspective here. 

I'd push back on what I perceive as you having conjugated this AA divergence as negative, threatening, or "like segwit".

Segwit/blocksize was a civil war within the monolithic Bitcoin L1. Two sides were competing over the same turf.

In contrast, the divergence of AA approaches between Base L2 and the L1 is a positive, healthy signal of ethereum's modular roadmap producing genuine differentiation. Here we have both L1 and L2 sticking to our/their respective values and strategy. Ethereum is stronger for it.

AA happened to be the first area to result in this chain-level protocol divergence between the L1 and a major L2. It might have been another area or another L2 instead of AA and Base.

This was always going to happen-- not in some fatalistic sense that the "cracks are showing"... rather as a warm, strong signal of the growing maturity and specialization of our L1 and L2s.

text:
How should we build long-horizon manipulation systems? As coding agents become more capable, what interface should connect models to the physical world? We’ve been thinking about this since 2024.

Introducing Retriever, a programming framework for asynchronous, closed-loop robot systems, built over the past year at Stanford and Northeastern.

- Robot agents run in physical time with various feedback loops, currently lacking a good programming abstraction.
- Retriever introduces a time-aware building block, “Flow”, analogous to a PyTorch layer or a Ray Actor.
- Users connect Flows and specify when each runs and what inputs it reads. Retriever handles asynchronous execution.
- Agents are represented as directed graphs with temporal feedback loops for closed-loop, hierarchical systems, decoupling algorithm logic from execution.

We built Retriever-0 agent to demonstrate long-horizon, partially observable tasks combining perception, memory, reasoning, and manipulation.

Here's the system in action. Paper, code, and demos below.

quoted_text:
honestly still wrapping my head around the past 24h

from whitepaper to launch, we tried to adapt with the level of interest, never would i have imagined this protocol would be the most liquid token on robinhood from day 1

while there may have been some things we couldve done better, i think we did a lot of things right and id like to go over those

first, we knew how much attention this launch would get and we needed to be super vigilant about botting and sniping that would be an existential threat to the entire protocol

we looked over different methods, simulated different scenarios internally and landed on what we thought was a solid solution

fake endpoints labeled 'launch keys' for early site crawlers looking for any edge, cloudflare turnstile to prove users were human, and a secret cloudflare worker that only propagated to production 10 seconds before launch so botters wouldnt have enough time to change their infra

this seemed to deter most, if not all botting on the charter auctions as many manual clickers got to mint and some even minting multiple

we have a 94% unique holder count which is mind boggling for the level of hype and attention around this launch 🤯

maybe optimistic to say but, maybe this can be a new standard (no pun intended) for future projects..?

the launch tax worked incredibly well, no single person scooped an existential amount and it bolstered the protocols treasury. the tax was almost like a da for the opening token price

we ran into some issues with DEX routers but we are getting all that resolved, routing v4 hooks is quite the challenge so please give everyone some patience

overall, this is just day 1 and we have some neat things coming!!

appreciate all the support and stay tuned

text:
The CLARITY Act failed to advance in the U.S. Senate today, falling short of the 60 votes needed to move forward.

We are disappointed by this outcome: legislation would future-proof crypto policy in the U.S. However, this does not affect how tokenized securities will operate in the U.S. They already fall within the federal securities framework, and Securitize has spent years building regulated infrastructure for issuance, transfer agency, trading, and fund administration of real securities onchain, not synthetic or derivative versions of them.

Furthermore, we expect the SEC and CFTC to proceed with agency rulemaking that will advance crypto and other policies. While not as durable as legislation, we anticipate a path forward in the most critical areas will be forthcoming.

We will continue to support the CLARITY Act and other efforts to establish durable market-structure rules for crypto. We will also continue working with lawmakers, regulators, issuers, and market participants to further advance the ecosystem for tokenized securities in the U.S.

Clear legislation can give institutions greater certainty across administrations. In the meantime, Securitize will continue building the infrastructure that brings securities and capital markets onchain.

Tokenize the World.

text:
vitalik connecting crypto mechanism design to AI safety is probably the cleanest framing we got this year

the core insight is a structural duality:

in crypto governance: simple algorithms trying to constrain smarter, adversarial human agents.

in AI safety: simpler principals (humans / weaker models) trying to constrain smarter, adversarial LLMs.

multi-agent AI failure modes aren't just single rogue models.
it's unauthorized agent-to-agent collusion under misalignment.

we spent a decade building anti-collusion, verification, and game-theoretic checks for onchain governance.

turns out that same mechanism design toolkit is directly portable to agentic harnesses.

governance isn't just for DAOs anymore. it's AI containment infrastructure.

🫡
https://t.co/fheAok369R
author: JakeHartnell
quoted_text:
It's possible that a killer app of adversarial governance mechanism design theory will end up being AI safety.

Compare:

https://t.co/w2LeAoVysF

https://t.co/dZXnORP9LU

There's a deep duality between the two environments. Both are about a less-sophisticated principal trying to get ideal outcomes from a set of more-sophisticated agents: in the first case, the principal is a static algorithm and the agents are humans, in the second case, the principal is humans plus weaker LLMs and the agents are stronger LLMs.

A key finding was that you can achieve much better outcomes if you can guarantee limits to how much agents can collude (see: Nash equilibria being abundant, vs. cooperative-game-theory "cores" often being empty). That argument should naturally transfer to this new setting.

text:
honestly still wrapping my head around the past 24h

from whitepaper to launch, we tried to adapt with the level of interest, never would i have imagined this protocol would be the most liquid token on robinhood from day 1

while there may have been some things we couldve done better, i think we did a lot of things right and id like to go over those

first, we knew how much attention this launch would get and we needed to be super vigilant about botting and sniping that would be an existential threat to the entire protocol

we looked over different methods, simulated different scenarios internally and landed on what we thought was a solid solution

fake endpoints labeled 'launch keys' for early site crawlers looking for any edge, cloudflare turnstile to prove users were human, and a secret cloudflare worker that only propagated to production 10 seconds before launch so botters wouldnt have enough time to change their infra

this seemed to deter most, if not all botting on the charter auctions as many manual clickers got to mint and some even minting multiple

we have a 94% unique holder count which is mind boggling for the level of hype and attention around this launch 🤯

maybe optimistic to say but, maybe this can be a new standard (no pun intended) for future projects..?

the launch tax worked incredibly well, no single person scooped an existential amount and it bolstered the protocols treasury. the tax was almost like a da for the opening token price

we ran into some issues with DEX routers but we are getting all that resolved, routing v4 hooks is quite the challenge so please give everyone some patience

overall, this is just day 1 and we have some neat things coming!!

appreciate all the support and stay tuned
