author: protocollabs
quoted_text:
We built recursive meta-intelligence, an AI that creates its own scientific instruments, turns them into persistent worlds that an agent ecology with hundreds of AIs inhabits, and uses those worlds to discover mechanistic principles in one of the hardest classes of physical problems: how complex hierarchical materials (nested structures of matter that give rise to new function through organization) evolve and fail. The AI reasons across enormous spaces of possible physical trajectories, where every rupture changes what can happen next, and compresses those histories into principles (which humans can understand and design with) - complex chains of causal events, highly nonlinear, and intricate. 

Scientific superintelligence is tangible here - machine-scale exploration opening cognitive channels into complexity that has been extremely difficult for humans to traverse directly. AI builds the spaces in which its next level of reasoning becomes possible; a representation becomes an instrument, the instrument becomes an executable world, and that world becomes the substrate for further intelligence. Intelligence then grows by constructing new spaces to think in.

The task we explored started from a seemingly simple prompt to explore a biological material system - the AI then chose the representation, mechanics and experiments, built a fracture laboratory to push materials to their limit, tested hypotheses and generated scientific conclusions. The swarm explored a combinatorial universe in which architecture controls function and every rupture changes the future state of the material.

The AI discovered a compact principle that defines how multiscale material architecture can program the evolution of failure. Material placement and geometric order determine how forces redistribute, whether damage cascades or remains distributed, and whether function survives substantial flaws. For this discovery to happen the AI had to reason across long path-dependent histories, simulate alternative futures and compress them into generative invariants (model-based causal reasoning, counterfactual simulation and temporal abstraction applied to an evolving physical world). It is incredible to witness this transition to a new form of intelligence and capability through scaling swarms.

A lot of positive will come out of this because it expands the human epistemic horizon as AI can traverse thousands of possible histories and return mechanisms compact enough for us to understand, test and build from. Intelligence compounds through its artifacts!

A few lessons we learned:

▶️ Learning and discovery are flows through spaces of possibility. Early work has shown how backpropagation flows through parameters, reinforcement learning through action and consequence, and autonomous swarms through representations, instruments and executable worlds, bringing it all together. Flows create structure; structure redirects future flows in the recursive instrument.

▶️ Nonlinear physics actually defines a larger principle, where high-dimensional dynamics generate stable invariants; invariants become effective variables; those variables become the substrate for a new level of cognition. 

▶️ Recursion then becomes level creation - one possibility space compresses into a principle, and that principle opens a larger space above it.

author: nicoypei
quoted_text:
I’ve really been enjoying Instinct, a personal AI agent. The simplest description for it is: OpenClaw for normal people.

It feels like magic. And contrary to what some people have said, I don’t think the appeal is limited to Silicon Valley types, we are setting my dad up with it too.

I’ve exchanged 677 messages with Instinct in the past five days. Here are some of the things it has done for me:

1) I asked who I should see about fixing my flat feet. It recommended starting with a podiatrist, found a well-reviewed one who takes my insurance, and filled out all the paperwork for me. I HATE finding in-network doctors, so this is a great use case for me.
2) It helped decrease my Comcast bill from $100/month to $60/month. It hit a wall on this one but gave me a number to call and an exact script. The call took three minutes.
3) We’re ordering custom merch for my brother’s wedding. It found vendors and is messaging several of them on WhatsApp- asking questions, comparing options, and negotiating prices while I’m asleep because the vendors are in India.
4) I’m planning his bachelor party. Everyone posted their arrival details in a WhatsApp group, so I asked Instinct to organize everything in a spreadsheet. It has access to my WhatsApp, so there was nothing for me to copy and paste.
5) My wife and I are going a wellness retreat (Miraval) in a couple of weeks, where many of the activities need to be booked in advance. After some back-and-forth about what we’d enjoy, Instinct researched the highest-rated activities and booked them for us. Massage slots appeared to be unavailable online, so it emailed the hotel from my account, found times that worked for us, and booked those too.
6) It did something similar for a girls’ trip my wife is taking with a friend, but booked very different activities for the two of them than it did for us.
7) It booked a DMV appointment for my new driver’s license.
8) It canceled all my Amazon Subscribe & Save subscriptions.
9) It activated all the free offers on my credit cards, just in case. I can't be bothered with those but if it's no work on my end there is no harm
10) It price-shopped my car insurance and concluded that I already have the best rate through Tesla.
11) My wife and I are traveling on the same United flight but booked on separate tickets. Instinct contacted United and linked our itineraries, a task that requires chatting with the airline and can’t be done through self-service.
12) It found and booked a factory tour at an Amazon fulfillment center that I'd been meaning to do, at a time that fit my calendar.
13) It suggested topics for a podcast I was appearing on. I didn’t end up using all of them, but they were pretty good.
14) It reminded me about a bunch of unused gift cards I had forgotten about.
15) I sent it a photo of a toll notice. It paid the toll, discovered another outstanding one, and paid that too.

None of these things is individually life-changing. Some of these things can be done via their own apps... But together, they represent hours of annoying life admin I didn’t have to do, and I have one easy place (imessage!) to do them.

There’s an obvious question: why doesn’t ChatGPT, or, Meta or Google already do all of this?

The underlying technology clearly exists- to use tools and complete multi-step tasks. But they haven't packaged it as a persistent personal operator with this level of access to your accounts and communications. The other AI's are also more cautious about purchases, cancellations, messages, and other external actions, so they will often stop for confirmation, which kills the vibe tbh! Note: I haven't been playing with Grok Bot yet, which I think does a lot of this.

A year ago I thought memory was the killer feature and it was awesome that ChatGPT had it, but Meta and Google had even more context / a natural advantage that they could ride on to be your personal AI agent. Meta's data with WhatsApp, etc...; Google with Gmail, Calendar, Chrome, and Android. 

But I've found the data that Instinct gets from being connected to your email to be pretty sufficient to get started and it can fill in the gaps. 

And the amount of context Google/Meta have that could make their assistants incredibly useful would also create enormous privacy, compliance, and trust problems for them. Plenty of people are uncomfortable giving those companies this much visibility into their lives, lawyers and lawmakers would come after them like crazy... not to mention there are probably all sorts of T&C's that Instinct is breaking. It is a bit scary how much information Instinct has and what it can do. We're going to start to see a new excuse: "I didn't send that email, it was my AI assistant" 

Anyway, good opening for Instinct. Much less about having a uniquely capable model and more about the product harness around it: integrations, permissions, context, persistence, willingness to keep working until the task is finished.

Something like: ChatGPT/Claude still feel like assistants that you operate, but Instinct is an assistant you employ.

Very cool product. It has the potential to make life easier for a lot of people. Excited to see more develop here.

And if you want to sign up go here: https://t.co/Nu8pNhKyiM currently on waitlist. I don't have any more invites. I gave out 100+ invites on here and they were taken in 2 mins. If I get more I'll post them!

text:
1/4

Solving math problems does not automatically solve code verification. The claim that AI can verify code just by compiling it to math is too simplistic. Naive, really, and insulting for generations of Turing award winners who moved from mathematics to computer science precisely to solve this highly-nontrivial problem.

Programs have control flow, state and structure that an algorithm can exploit. Leaving everything to general theorem search is leaving that structure unused. Code reasoning should organize the proof: follow execution, split cases, summarize loops, and call mathematical provers on the obligations that arise.

More than 50 years of verification research has gone into developing this machinery. Progress in AI math/code should build on that foundation.

quoted_text:
Last month I wrote about how we can build a positive and safe future for everyone: https://t.co/eoLGVY8yad

Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens.

The reality is:

- People won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask, so labs have a strong natural incentive to make their models more aligned.

There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up. My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind.

- Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.

Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us. I'm proud of the security foundations we've built.

- Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice. MSL already does this today in several areas because it helps produce better work. Other labs can just do this too. In general, it would be helpful for there to be a larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators.

- Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely. Meta has made this commitment and other labs can do this as well.

I believe the key to building a positive future for everyone is maintaining the right balance of power. This is within our power to do.

quoted_text:
Many of us have mentioned how the stablecoin yield debate playing out in Clarity, and the arguments made against yield by the bank trades, mirror the battle over money market funds in the 1970s. Well here's some proof.

Here's a letter submitted by the Independent Bankers Association of America (a predecessor to the ICBA) in a 1980 hearing of the Senate Banking committee on money market funds. 

As you can see, many of their arguments against stablecoins are almost verbatim a copy from what they argued back then: threat to deposits, harms lending, uniquely dangerous for smaller banks.

And we know today that argument was dead wrong. Money market balances grew parabolically into the trillions, and yet banks remain flush with deposits.

text: Selective disclosure is what makes a public network usable for regulated finance.
author: CantonNetwork
quoted_text:
Privacy does not mean anonymity.

 In institutional finance, it means controlled visibility: payroll must not expose employee compensation; lending must not broadcast borrower positions; trading must not leak counterparties, pricing, or strategy.

 Canton’s model is need-to-know by design.

 Daml contracts define which parties receive each part of a transaction. In a delivery-versus-payment flow, a bank can receive cash-leg data without seeing securities details; a registrar can receive securities-leg data without receiving the cash movement. Relevant parties still validate and settle one atomic transaction.

 Compliance does not disappear under this model. Access can be programmatically granted to authorized parties under defined conditions, making disclosure controlled and auditable rather than public by default.

 That distinction matters: public network, private business data, verifiable settlement.  
 .@CantonNetwork

text:
上礼拜刚刚和 @0xPickleCati 聊完脑机接口的事情，转头就看到 @cyodyssey 老师和 @cz_binance 大表哥讨论基于 @BNBCHAIN 实现的数字永生。

仔细一想，这或许确实是区块链在未来最大的应用场景之一。

看到这里的讨论，我最先想起来的是星际迷航里面的“瞬间移动”理论。即，将人类转化为量子，瞬间移动到另外一个地方。这里比较出名的悖论就是，这种技术转移出来的人，是否仍然是之前那个人。

乍一听，这确实像是一个忒修斯之船一类，关于唯一性的问题，然而，在永生这个话题上，更重要的问题实际上在于意识的不可修改性和不可替代性。

举例而言：

- 假设我的意识被数据化了，我怎么知道我的记忆中是否有虚构的部分。假设有虚构的部分，那我是否仍然是我？

- 假设我通过数据化的资料实现了永生，我能否继承我的意识，即，我是否能够感知自己的永生，并让永生继续下去。

- 假设我的大脑资料可以无限次fork，那么到底哪一个fork的个体才能算是我，我原本意识的重要性又在哪里？

而这正是区块链一直以来正在解决的问题。

大家不要觉得这些问题是天方夜谭。我觉得这些问题其实比我们想象中的要近很多很多。

AI时代之后，现有的人机交互体系已经不足以最大化人类的工作能力。脑机接口，或者用更浪漫的说法来说，“电子脑”，将会是必然的大趋势。

而电子脑必然会带来一定程度上赛博永生，从而必然带来我们人类在独一性和存在主义上的危机。

在此前 @AnthropicAI 发表的文章中，我们也绝对不难看出，在电子脑出现之前，这一独一性已经因为AI带来的广阔的网络效应，开始受到威胁。（这里大家可以看一下 @0xPickleCati 之前吐槽Anthropic的文章，即人类的灵魂，正在以AI这一共同的接口，不断同化。）

说回区块链。

当人类的大脑与网络的完全接轨已经无法避免，当我们的自我独一性开始逐渐消亡时，所有权，隐私，数据隔离，将会比任何时候都要重要。

当我们的灵魂将被数字化的时候，至少我会希望，我的灵魂仍然是我的灵魂。

最后，我想简单讲讲在刚刚完结的重制版攻壳机动队中，关于这件事情的反思。

简单做一下梗概 - 剧情里面有一个吸收了网络上所有的资讯，由互联网诞生的数字生命体。在故事的最后，这个近乎完美的数字生命体，却选择和保有电子灵魂的主角融合。

融合的原因很简单 - 不论这个数字生命体如何进化，如何fork，它进化的终点时统一的，是缺乏个性和多样性的。在反复的融合与进化之下，信息集合体和单个的fork分支不会存在任何的区别。

相比之下，人类的个性，独一性，将会是未来唯一有价值的东西。

而在这个未来里，我们便有机会见到区块链成为这最终价值的载体。成为不灭灵魂的唯一佐证。

author: jbrukh
quoted_text:
Last month I wrote about how we can build a positive and safe future for everyone: https://t.co/eoLGVY8yad

Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens.

The reality is:

- People won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask, so labs have a strong natural incentive to make their models more aligned.

There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up. My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind.

- Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.

Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us. I'm proud of the security foundations we've built.

- Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice. MSL already does this today in several areas because it helps produce better work. Other labs can just do this too. In general, it would be helpful for there to be a larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators.

- Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely. Meta has made this commitment and other labs can do this as well.

I believe the key to building a positive future for everyone is maintaining the right balance of power. This is within our power to do.

By stripping out generative prose entirely they hit wild 150ms response times:

IMO this is an incredibly smart way to route logic without paying for words you do not need 👀

author: ccatalini
quoted_text:
Last month I wrote about how we can build a positive and safe future for everyone: https://t.co/eoLGVY8yad

Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens.

The reality is:

- People won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask, so labs have a strong natural incentive to make their models more aligned.

There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up. My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind.

- Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.

Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us. I'm proud of the security foundations we've built.

- Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice. MSL already does this today in several areas because it helps produce better work. Other labs can just do this too. In general, it would be helpful for there to be a larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators.

- Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely. Meta has made this commitment and other labs can do this as well.

I believe the key to building a positive future for everyone is maintaining the right balance of power. This is within our power to do.

OG NFT builders are back, and it feels like @CryptoKitties season but on @RobinhoodCrypto this time. 

@MeebitsNFTs, a @doodles co-founder, and Abstract's top game dev all launched on Robinhood in the same week. 

We break down how NFTs seem to be making a comeback on Robinhood chain with a common inspiration in robinhood:0xe934e36a439c94017b64a3fece66af12099abf50.

If this trend continues, expect a 2nd wave of NFT ↔️  DeFi ↔️ Gaming iterations to take off from here.
Top Robinhood NFT Projects That Can 100X! NFTFi Season IS HERE!

NFTs are back on our radar for the first time since Stonkbroker launched, and it's happening on Robinhood. In this one, we break down the wave of NFT experiments that all launched within days of each other, and why we think Stonkbrokers lit the fuse that brought the OG builders out of hibernation.

We start with Nightshades, the @MeebitsNFTs comeback built on Stonk Launcher: four competing factions, each with its own NFT collection and token, a 99 percent anti-snipe tax that feeds ETH back into the game, and a nightly @chainlink VRF roll that decides which factions take damage. All four tokens bonded with nearly $500K in volume and a combined $1.2M market cap out of the gate.

From there we get into the new batch of NFT projects everyone should have on the radar. @RareFriendsNFT is the Doodles co-founder's fully on-chain experiment, with artwork, payouts, and even animations rendered in @solidity_lang, launching through a continuous clearing auction that was already implying a $13M market cap. @standard_rsv is the new OHM-flavored reserve asset that raised $1.5M and immediately showed $15M in liquidity, and we walk through where that number actually comes from and the caveat hiding in the hook logic. @YieldFields_RH is a land deed farming game from the team behind one of Abstract's biggest games, and @hashcats_rh brings back proof-of-work nostalgia with NFTs you mine from your browser instead of buying.

The thread connecting all of it is that these aren't anonymous forks chasing a trend. Meebits, a Doodles co-founder, and proven game builders are all choosing Robinhood at the same time, and each one is recycling fees into a flywheel instead of extracting them. That tells us the chain has become the place where NFT natives think the next real experiment gets rewarded, and the speed at which the market is absorbing these launches backs that up.

Where we land is that NFTs, not tokens, are the more likely vehicle to pull mainstream users into this cycle. A launchpad coin can run to a billion, but a character you keep alive, a plot of land you farm, or a cat you mined yourself is an experience people actually understand. If these experiments start plugging real-world assets and commodities into that gameplay, the RWA meta and the NFT meta stop being separate stories, and that intersection is the thing we'd be watching most closely from here.

text:
Google has released Gemini 3.8 Live, its new Speech to Speech model, with the Extended Thinking (High) variant debuting at #1 on the Artificial Analysis Speech to Speech Index at 82.6, and #1 on our Tau Voice benchmark implementation at 68.6%

Gemini 3.8 Live is @GoogleDeepMind's successor to Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, a Speech to Speech model that executes tools and API calls in the background while continuing the conversation. It comes in two variants: the standard Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking, which supports configurable reasoning effort. We evaluated the standard model and the Extended Thinking variant at High reasoning effort through the Gemini Live API.

Key takeaways:
➤ Speech to Speech Index: Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) debuts at #1 at 82.6, ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 81.5, Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 81.3 and GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 80.1. The standard Gemini 3.8 Live debuts at #5 at 76.0, with both variants up on Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High at 71.5 (+11.1 and +4.5 points). The Index averages Speech Reasoning (Big Bench Audio), Agentic Performance (Tau Voice), Arena Preference and Arena Task Success Rate
➤ Speech Agent Arena: Gemini 3.8 Live ranks #2 in preference at Elo 1083, behind Gemini 3.1 Flash Live (1096) and ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1053, and #2 on Task Success Rate at 93.2%, behind Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 94.6%. Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) trails at Elo 990 with 89.1% task success
➤ Tau Voice: Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) takes the top spot on our Tau Voice benchmark implementation at 68.6%, ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 67.9%, GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 59.3% and Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 56.5% - up from 37.7% for Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High. The standard Gemini 3.8 Live scores 30.1%
➤ Big Bench Audio: Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) scores 97.7% on audio reasoning, ahead of Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 97.2% and behind Qwen Audio 3.0 Realtime Plus at 99.2%. The standard Gemini 3.8 Live scores 91.7%
➤ Speed: Average Time to First Audio on Big Bench Audio is 1.18 seconds for Gemini 3.8 Live and 1.35 seconds for Extended Thinking (High), both well ahead of Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High (2.99s) and in line with GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1.24s and GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 1.34s, though behind Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 0.70s
➤ Cost: Gemini 3.8 Live costs $0.84 per hour of input audio, the cheapest model in the Index and roughly half the $1.75 of Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High. Extended Thinking (High) costs $3.50 per hour - cheaper than GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at $4.47, Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at $4.80 and GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at $5.83, and ~3.1x cheaper than GPT-Realtime-2.1 High at $10.75

See below for more detail ⬇️

Bitmine, the largest Ethereum-focused digital asset treasury firm, bought another 27,180 ETH last week — roughly $68 million at Monday's ether price just above $2,500 — bringing its holdings to 5,956,378 ETH. With ether's supply around 122 million tokens, the company needs about 144,000 more ETH to reach its goal of cornering 5% of supply, or 6.1 million tokens. Buying held at roughly the same pace as the prior week, and Bitmine has added ether every week since starting its Ethereum treasury strategy in June 2025.

Chairman Tom Lee, founder of Fundstrat, pointed to several possible catalysts for further ETH upside into the final months of the year. He said the ETH-BTC ratio reached its highest level since Jan. 30 and broke above a downtrend in place since 2022. "In our view, this reflects Ethereum's strengthened position as the settlement rails for Wall Street tokenization and the increased realization that Ethereum may play a critical central role in managing agentic-AI," Lee said.

Lee also cited a Senate vote on U.S. crypto market-structure legislation, best known as the Clarity Act, currently expected Tuesday, along with renewed crypto buying from Korean investors. The target remains within sight if Bitmine keeps its current acquisition pace.

text:
The Clarity Act is dead.

Before the post-mortems and the planning sessions begin, a note of thanks.

Many of you worked extremely hard on this bill over the last 18 months. You fought harder than most people will ever know to make sure we had a good product that actually worked for crypto. It required countless hours of research and analysis; endless calls and meetings to build consensus; rewriting the same sections over and over to find common ground; winning points and making concessions one by one in pursuit of an ambitious goal.

Those efforts were a success. The bill did not pass, but neither did you compromise on your principles or the ultimate goal. It would have been easy to strike deal at any point by simply giving up and rolling over, and you were asked to do so every single day for 18 months. You did not. Your strength, courage, and confidence won the day. You should be proud.

Many of us said since the start of this process that no bill is better than a bad bill, and by that metric, today is a victory. The Senate considered a good bill today, not a perfect one but a good one, and turned it down. The raw politics of the United States during an election year meant a good deal was not on the table. That's okay.

Crypto will be fine without the Clarity Act. We are lucky to have two agencies, the SEC and CFTC, with all of the excellent staff and authority they need to do the job. They're ready to be unleashed, and so they shall be. The future of crypto policy is bright.

Thank you all for your hard work. Breathe a sigh of relief, take a break, and get ready for what's next. We've only just gotten started.

I have conducted an audit of Anthropic's finances.

What I have found is so shocking that I am calling for a Congressional investigation.

Anthropic is not just seeking regulatory capture.

It has built a regulatory capture machine that cannot be turned off.

Structural financial incentives make it impossible for Anthropic -- I call it the Anthropic Network -- to turn off its own AI doom cycle.

It starts with METR.

Dario Amodei proposes "third-party evaluators" to assess the risk of Anthropic's models.

He proposes METR for this purpose.

But METR is financially dependent on the Anthropic's success -- specifically, on the explosive growth of more than $7 billion dollars in Anthropic stock.

Dustin Moskovitz invested this stock into Good Ventures Foundation, where it represents the majority of that organization's portfolio.

And GVF is the overwhelming funder of the entire Anthropic Network ecosystem.

This stock was worth $500 million early last year.

It is worth more than $7.7 billion just ~16 months later.

METR -- and all of those building a career its parent organizations -- cannot afford to disrupt that growth.

Because if Anthropic goes under, many of the organizations that fund METR go under as well.

But if Anthropic succeeds, METR and its parent organizations become more richly financed to regulate AI -- something those at METR want very much.

The "third-party evaluator" is not "third-party" at all.

The evaluator is on Anthropic's payroll.

If this were the end of it, that's bad.

But that isn't all.

The same organizations that fund METR also fund the many organizations, such as the Tarbell Center, that promote AI Doom.

The Tarbell Center publishes AI Doom articles in The Verge, Science, LA Times, The Dispatch, TIME, and others.

They are selling the problem, and then selling the solution to the problem -- from the same money pile: Anthropic's.

All of these organizations are financially dependent on the same exploding $7 billion money pile.

As Anthropic grows more and more powerful, its AI Doom Machine grows better and better financed -- louder and louder.

Meanwhile, the regulatory regime seeded in METR grows larger to solve the increasingly loud -- now hysterical -- problem of AI Doom that the Anthropic Network itself created.

From this standpoint, as Anthropic becomes more powerful, AI might be getting scarier, sure -- but the positive feedback loop also becomes more deafening -- independent of objective facts.

This itself is an objective fact.

The deafening AI Doom is part of an business model, that, as it expands, so too does the AI Doom messaging -- there is simply more money to do it.

But the problem also goes in the other direction:

If Anthropic dies, the Regulatory Regime and the AI Doom Machine are crippled or die.

Neither METR nor Tarbell nor the other organizations in the Anthropic Network can allow that to happen.

Hence, neither METR or the AI Doom Machine can be trusted to provide independent assessments of Anthropic's models or AI more broadly.

They simply are not organizations independent of Anthropic.

And Anthropic cannot detach itself from METR or Tarbell or countless other safety orgs (not shown here), either, because they drive hype for the models and the possibility of eventual regulatory capture, and Anthropic will not give that up willingly.

What's more, the people at all of these organizations are all the same ecosystem, the same community. They just shuffle between organizations.

The Anthropic Network is therefore, so long as it is successful, locked into a self-amplifying feedback loop inside an ideological monoculture.

And that feedback loop is winning.

That's what Jacob Coxon is.

China is keeping messaging tight. That is why optimism for AI is so high in China.

America has Anthropic: a massive company pushing anti-AI propaganda at a state level.

Anthropic will either create hysteria until American AI slows down and China wins, or it will create fractures throughout American society with severe political consequences.

Ironically, because of the structural financial incentives underpinning the Anthropic Network, it has become the same kind of self-amplifying virus that it fantasizes AI to become in the future -- while hiding its tracks just as carefully.

It is the mirror of the same AI virus that it hypothesizes to consume America.

Anthropic's business model, models itself after the very thing it claims to fear.

Except Anthropic's ideology infects humans, not computers.

Congress must investigate.

quoted_text:
Peter Thiel on why the name of your startup is predictive of success or failure

“This is a slight aesthetic thing that I believe in very strongly: the names of companies are often very predictive of future failure or success.”

PayPal and Napster are the first example Thiel gives:

“PayPal was a very friendly name — it was the friend that helps you pay. Napster was a bad name — you nap some music, you nap a kid. That sounds like a bad thing to be doing, and it’s no wonder the government then comes in and shuts the company down within a few years.”

“You want to be very careful of how you name companies,” Thiel warns founders. In the context of the sharing economy, he likes Airbnb more than Uber:

“Airbnb sounds very innocent like this virtual bread and breakfast — this very light, non-threatening sort of company. Uber sounds like a bad name from Germany sometime in the 1930s. What are you exactly above? Maybe the law? This is probably something that, again from a regulatory perspective, I think Airbnb is a vastly better name than Uber.”

And on the social networking side, Thiel likes Facebook more than MySpace:

“You can say that all these social networks involve both reading and writing… Over time, reading dominates writing. Facebook was about learning about people around you — about their real identities at Harvard. MySpace started among wannabe actors in Los Angeles, and it was about them coming up with fictional narratives around themselves and a lot of other people in LA who are generally like that. And because reading dominates writing, Facebook would ultimately dominate MySpace. There’s a certain version where the whole arc of the company and the whole product arc was implicit in the names.”

Source: @mercatus (Apr 2015)

author: martin_casado
quoted_text:
Last month I wrote about how we can build a positive and safe future for everyone: https://t.co/eoLGVY8yad

Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens.

The reality is:

- People won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask, so labs have a strong natural incentive to make their models more aligned.

There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up. My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind.

- Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.

Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us. I'm proud of the security foundations we've built.

- Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice. MSL already does this today in several areas because it helps produce better work. Other labs can just do this too. In general, it would be helpful for there to be a larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators.

- Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely. Meta has made this commitment and other labs can do this as well.

I believe the key to building a positive future for everyone is maintaining the right balance of power. This is within our power to do.

quoted_text:
Last month I wrote about how we can build a positive and safe future for everyone: https://t.co/eoLGVY8yad

Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens.

The reality is:

- People won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask, so labs have a strong natural incentive to make their models more aligned.

There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up. My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind.

- Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.

Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us. I'm proud of the security foundations we've built.

- Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice. MSL already does this today in several areas because it helps produce better work. Other labs can just do this too. In general, it would be helpful for there to be a larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators.

- Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely. Meta has made this commitment and other labs can do this as well.

I believe the key to building a positive future for everyone is maintaining the right balance of power. This is within our power to do.

2017–2021：
Crypto 是从抵制到暧昧。

2021-2025:
从暧昧到公开支持全面发展。

2025–2026：
Crypto 成为需要被规范的新产业。

其次，白宫已经明确表示，如果国会失败，SEC 和 CFTC 仍会继续利用现有规则制定权推进监管框架。

双方现在争论的是 guardrails，而已经不是 Crypto 是否应该存在，Crypto 存在并且发展已经是不争的事实。

text:
刚看到一个挺新鲜的模型 Jev，这是一个专门帮程序做选择题的 AI。

比如一个 AI Agent 刚帮你处理完一封退款邮件，程序接下来有四个选择：

退款
拒绝退款
再问用户一个问题
转给人工

GPT、Claude 这种模型，一般会读完邮件，然后生成一段文字告诉你「我认为应该退款，因为……」。

Jev 不写这段话。

你直接把这四个选项丢给它，它返回：

退款 82%
拒绝 3%
继续询问 10%
转人工 5%

程序看到结果，直接执行下一步。

所以可以把 Jev 理解成一个给软件和 Agent 用的超级分类器 / 判断器。它不擅长陪你聊天，也不是拿来写文章、写代码的。它专门处理那种答案范围已经确定，只需要 AI 快速判断「选哪个」的问题。

这类问题其实在 Agent 里特别多。

任务做完没有？
这个结果合不合格？
下一步调用哪个工具？
需不需要重试？
有没有触发风险规则？
该不该交给人工？

现在很多 Agent 都是每遇到一次这种问题，就喊 GPT、Claude 出来跑一遍。哪怕最后只需要一个 YES / NO，大模型还是要走完整套生成流程。

Jev 就专门把这部分拿出来做。

做它的 TypeSafe AI 创始人 Diogo Almeida 以前在 OpenAI，参与过 InstructGPT 和 RLHF，后来这套东西一路变成了 ChatGPT。TypeSafe 做了两年刚出 stealth，同时拿了 4000 万美元 seed。

他们给 Jev 的定位也很明确：大量、重复、结构化的 AI 判断。

所以它追求的东西和 GPT-6、Claude 完全不同，核心就是快和便宜。

TypeSafe 自己公布的数据是，在适合 Jev 的工作流里，速度可以快 20–200 倍，成本低 40–400 倍，100 万输入 token 只要 0.042 美元。

第三方 Every 也测了一轮。

他们让 Jev 和 Fable 5.1 检查文章问题。Jev 单篇中位耗时 0.35 秒，Fable 是 8.83 秒，差不多快 25 倍。另一个测试里，Jev 在 0.7 秒内给 37 篇文章分别做了 21 项判断，一共 777 个判断，成本只有大概四分之一美分。

准确率会有交换。一次测试里，Fable 找出了 7 个问题，Jev 找到了 6 个。

我觉得 Jev 真正值得看的就是这里。

现在大家做 Agent，经常默认每一个需要“智能”的地方都塞一个大语言模型进去。以后可能会拆得越来越细。

真正需要理解复杂问题、规划、写代码的地方，用 GPT、Claude。

中间那些成千上万次「对不对」「选哪个」「要不要继续」的判断，交给 Jev 这种模型。

如果未来 Agent 真开始一天替人跑几百上千个任务，这种模型可能会变得很重要。

This FOMO hate is a fair convo to have.. but at this point I think people are misplacing the blame 

If Coinbase PnLs were public we would have seen this 8 years ago even in 2017 or 2021 cycles

The harsh truth is: most people fomo buy and panic sell. They chase 100X PnLs and have no idea why they are buying anything in the first place. 

This is NOT unique to crypto, it's basic human nature

The majority of PROFESSIONAL HEDGE FUNDS lose money!!! 

Literal pros. Does that make CNBC unethical? Is the economy simply "bad?"

Total % profitable is a terrible metric because people are absolutely terrible at managing capital 

FOMO is at least showing mainstream interest in onchain token buying

FOMO is bringing real users to crypto for the first time

text: “Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us.”
author: chamath
quoted_text:
Last month I wrote about how we can build a positive and safe future for everyone: https://t.co/eoLGVY8yad

Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens.

The reality is:

- People won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask, so labs have a strong natural incentive to make their models more aligned.

There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up. My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind.

- Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.

Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us. I'm proud of the security foundations we've built.

- Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice. MSL already does this today in several areas because it helps produce better work. Other labs can just do this too. In general, it would be helpful for there to be a larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators.

- Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely. Meta has made this commitment and other labs can do this as well.

I believe the key to building a positive future for everyone is maintaining the right balance of power. This is within our power to do.

Important updates on @Revolut and what you can do:

1. According to the group now extorting Revolut, and to the Duel team in contact with them, the attackers took over Italian government and law enforcement mailboxes with an infostealer, sent Revolut Bank UAB in Lithuania a forged European Investigation Order (to attention of @Eurojust @Europol ) in the name of the Italian authorities, and kept sending requests for five months. 

2. Revolut answered every one, as @FATFNews and EU AML laws require. Now scale this abuse a thousand times, in the hands of authoritarian states and their proxies, who do not seek attention like these hackers and quietly collect data on citizens and entities of the EU and other Western countries.

3. The attackers claim to hold 147 GB from the Italian side, including internal documents and officer chat logs, and say most of the Revolut data concerns customers in Switzerland, France and Hungary, with other countries affected. Passports and KYC selfies of named individuals are now being published daily until Revolut pays. 

We are collecting witness statements to push for remedies. If you are a legal or security expert and want to support our team, DM me.

What you as an EU citizen can do today to limit these attacks in the future: 

1. Contact your MEP on @EP_Economics, @EP_Legal or @EP_Justice and ask for an urgent joint hearing on the weaponisation of mass data collection and a reassessment of the whole approach, before the next leak names someone who does not have the means to move house. 

2. Use this argument: every bank, exchange and payment provider in every jurisdiction that follows FATF rules, and the AML, financial and national security laws built on them, is exposed the same way, because the rules oblige them to answer state requests and nobody is required to check whether the state behind the request is who it claims to be. 

That is what human rights groups, victims and experts with support of @ODFoundation described to the European Parliament three years ago, proposing specific remedies. The @EU_Commission and the @EUCouncil removed every safeguard the @Europarl_EN adopted from the AML Regulation.

3. You want politicians care more about privacy and digital rights protection? 

Support and promote the MPs and MEPs who pushed for remedies. Demand accountability for rejected remedies by Commission and Council. 

This year the European Parliament, under @HNeumannMEP @petras_petras @NachoSAmor leadership , named this risk transnational financial repression in its resolution of 18 June 2026. 

@coe adopted Resolution 2669 on 25 June, rapporteur @constantinosefs , with @MarkusWiechel pushing specifically for an investigation into transnational financial repression and remedies against it. 

The @oscepa followed in The Hague in July, led by @emmedibi , with an even more detailed focus on exactly these attacks.

author: Hesamation
quoted_text:
Last month I wrote about how we can build a positive and safe future for everyone: https://t.co/eoLGVY8yad

Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens.

The reality is:

- People won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask, so labs have a strong natural incentive to make their models more aligned.

There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up. My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind.

- Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.

Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us. I'm proud of the security foundations we've built.

- Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice. MSL already does this today in several areas because it helps produce better work. Other labs can just do this too. In general, it would be helpful for there to be a larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators.

- Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely. Meta has made this commitment and other labs can do this as well.

I believe the key to building a positive future for everyone is maintaining the right balance of power. This is within our power to do.

text:
Twenty-one of the world's largest banks are building a dollar stablecoin that, by law, cannot pay its holders a cent, and that ban is a reason they want to build it.

On September 1, a consortium including @GoldmanSachs, @Citi, @BankofAmerica, @DeutscheBank, @UBS, and MUFG confirmed plans to form a company this year and bring a GENIUS Act-compliant USD stablecoin to market in H1 2027, on public chains.

Under GENIUS, a payment stablecoin issuer cannot pass any yield to holders.

For a crypto-native issuer that is a handicap; for these banks it removes the one axis where a newcomer could undercut them and moves the contest to settlement and distribution, where incumbents already win.

> 21 banks, including Goldman, Citi, BofA, Deutsche, UBS, MUFG
> USD token targeted for H1 2027, on public blockchains
> GENIUS bars issuers from paying any yield to holders
> USDT and USDC still hold ~85% of a ~$303B stablecoin market . . .

The ban relocates the demand for yield rather than removing it. The reserve income these tokens throw off goes to the issuer, not the holder, so every dollar parked in one is a dollar whose owner still wants a return and has to earn it somewhere the token itself cannot provide.

The larger this non-yielding money layer grows, the larger the pool of capital sitting on top of it with nowhere to compound.

That capital looks for a compliant, risk-managed place to turn a parked balance into real return, a different job from issuing the dollar and a harder one than settling it.

One caveat: a three-party consortium structure may route yield indirectly, and regulators have moved to treat those arrangements as breaking the rule, so the line is not yet settled.

But the token itself still pays its holder nothing.

Smart money is watching where the yield on all this parked stablecoin ends up, because a bigger layer of money that cannot earn is the clearest signal yet of demand for the layer that makes it earn.

text:
We believe strongly in the necessity to invest into alignment.

1. People and businesses will only use agents that are aligned with their intent and values. If we do not build models aligned with people and businesses, then they will move to more aligned options.

2. Every lab should have a strong governance framework across training and deployment. This should include external evaluators, which are best practice for transparency, and independent oversight on things like safety criteria for model launches.

3. Every lab will need to operate within institutional protections of democratic countries. This means labs face significant liability if their models cause harm. This will push the ecosystem in the right ways.

4. Advances in the field are ultimately downstream of compute and resource allocation. Racing on recursive self-improvement is one of the riskiest pathways for potential loss of control to powerful models. Meta is committing the significant majority of our compute towards serving people rather than racing on RSI, and other labs can choose to do the same.

AI is a very powerful technology, and there is immense responsibility in developing it safely alongside the right checks and balances.

Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens.

The reality is:

- People won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask, so labs have a strong natural incentive to make their models more aligned.

There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up. My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind.

- Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.

Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us. I'm proud of the security foundations we've built.

- Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice. MSL already does this today in several areas because it helps produce better work. Other labs can just do this too. In general, it would be helpful for there to be a larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators.

- Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely. Meta has made this commitment and other labs can do this as well.

I believe the key to building a positive future for everyone is maintaining the right balance of power. This is within our power to do.

text:
Claude Code 2.1.273 带来了一个改变产品形态的更新：支持将远程控制会话 Fork 到本地后台。

这不是简单的后台挂起，而是带有完整状态保留的会话迁移。

这解决了一个核心痛点：运行耗时自动化任务时不再需要死守终端界面。
• UI 彻底解放：任务转入后台，当前终端界面直接释放。
• 状态无缝继承：原有的上下文和执行进度全部保留。

正如社区开发者所言，这个特性标志着 Claude Code 正在从“CLI 工具”向“Agent Runtime”演进——你可以离开终端，稍后再回来，而智能体仍在持续运转。

新版本（共计 64 项变更）还有两个非常实用的避坑升级：

• MCP 降级通知：修复了此前 MCP 断连导致任务默默失败的痛点，现在中途断开会明确通知，并支持 /mcp diagnostics 诊断。
• Auto 模式优化：在云端/远程会话中，Artifact 上传文件时自动化流程不再被迫暂停。

text: The biggest mistake Israel made re 10/7 was not immediately sharing all of the videos from that day.
author: BillAckman
quoted_text:
⚠️ WARNING: EXTREMELY GRAPHIC IMAGERY ⚠️

This was a music festival. People drove out to the western Negev to hear a DJ and stand under cheap colored shade and drink from red fridges that still say Coca-Cola in the frame. By the time this camera is moving, the music is gone and the only question left on the audio is whether anyone lying there can still signal that they are alive.

I’ve watched a lot of October 7 footage, hours of it, most of it unpublicized due to the severity of the imagery and the families not wanting it out there, and I still cannot get used to how ordinary the ground looks. Plastic chairs. A leopard-print bag by an open car door. A poster about being environmentally friendly. Then the bodies in the same dirt, and soldiers walking the same ground because the people who did this had already left with the ones they wanted alive.

Propagandists talk about this day as being just “chaos” and “both sides” and a raid that got a little out of hand. 

This is not that. 

This is what a massacre looks like when it is finished with a field and has not yet finished with the country. This is what intent to kill anyone and everyone looks like. 

They came for civilians at a festival. Young unarmed students. That is the whole sentence. Everything after it is commentary.

text:
Most high earners are broke and don't know it. @ramit can prove it in one number. 

That number is your fixed cost ratio: how much of your income is committed before you make any other choices. Rent/mortgage, loan payments, bills and more. If your fixed cost ratio is 90% and above, Ramit says that you are effectively broke, whatever your salary is. 

And in Hong Kong and Singapore, there is a trap that makes it even worse. Your tax isn't withheld, that means your employer doesn't take your tax out of your paycheck. You get the full amount, spend against it and then a large tax bill lands months later. 

Almost nobody can tell you their fixed cost ratio, at least not within 20%. This number quietly decides how free or trapped you are. And almost nobody has ever actually seen it.

That's a clarity problem we need to solve.

text:
“我没想到这天会到来，MCP正在变得比CLI更适合Agent”

@trq212 对 MCP 的观点发生了质的变化，同时把今年一线构建者心照不宣的那张底牌，彻底摊在了桌面上。

为什么连以往最坚定的“给模型一台电脑、让它去敲 CLI”一派，也开始承认多数集成该做成 MCP？ 因为过去两年血淋淋的教训已经证明了：靠给 API 套个聊天框，或者把内部系统随手暴露成一堆 Tool，在模型和协议的迭代面前脆弱得不堪一击，因为上下文会被 50 个工具定义吃光、一次只能处理一条、长任务超时、写错文档没人审、换一版模型产品就死一批。

真正能在 Agent 时代拥有定价权的，从来不是模型，也不是 CLI 还是 MCP 这个口号， 而是包在模型外面、让人每天真的愿意用的那套 Company Brain，或者称之为 Harness：

1️⃣ 从产品维度看：它把空盒子聊天改成了开箱即用的工作台： 大模型无状态、会忘、也不懂公司内部的脏活； CLI 赢在模型本来就会用，MCP 赢在远程服务、权限、结构化对象和跨客户端分发。一套成熟的公司大脑，负责把最脏的业务逻辑封进框架，长任务怎么后台跑、断点怎么续？批量怎么一次拿齐？跨系统上下文怎么按需装载，而不是整页倒进去。用户面对的不再是一个需要反复教它做人的对话框， 而是一座能把重复工作压到原来十分之一的专业工作台。

2️⃣ 从技术维度看，它才是你搬不走的私有资产： 通用大模型只是租来的发动机，CLI 也只是它已经会开的旧方向盘。 真正值钱的是后来补上的那层驾驭装置：工具如何延迟加载、按需展开，而不是一上来撑爆上下文？ MCP 如何做成无状态函数，而不是小心伺候的会话进程？ 过滤和组合是该交给 Unix 管道，还是下沉成 tool 上的 query 参数？ 什么写入可以自动跑完，什么必须先讲清楚再等人审，错了如何回滚、每次调用如何按人留下日志？ Thariq 改口主要还是因为工具可以懒加载了、协议也变得无状态了，CLI 当年那些结构优势，在被好的 MCP 版本迭代慢慢补上。 这套把领域最佳实践和安全红线写成工程代码的脚手架，换模型也换不走。

3️⃣ 为什么这是不可逆的浪潮？ 旧软件要么继续当记录系统慢慢老死， 要么进化成 Agent 真正愿意用、也用得稳的领域底座。会接 MCP、会让模型敲命令行，已经不稀奇了； 懂得在后台任务、批量、可观测、读写分离、工具目录和上下文预算上一次做对， 才算拥有了属于自己的Agent技术栈。

大模型的单点智力正在被迅速拉平； 与其天天追哪家模型又刷榜、或者站队 CLI 还是 MCP， 不如先问一句：你们的公司大脑，Agent 到底愿不愿意用、用不用得稳。Harness 的浪潮已经到了生产层， 把内部工具箱做深的人，才配在这场长跑里拿到门票。

I was going to write this one for subscribers, but I have to make this for everyone because so many people still don't see the vision

I still think robinhood:0xaa07a0e9209e16ac99708c3ec70159c6ef3128a3 is the most asymmetric project on Robinhood Chain. This is a net-new vertical, with all the right levers in a world where AI demand is accelerating.

Yes, inference marketplaces have been tried in crypto. But none have worked at scale. With CREDIT, akin to DIEM, you now have succeeded at tokenizing inference. And in doing so, you basically unlock credits for an increasingly agentic world. Agents need fuel they can buy and use without a human in the loop; This is the start of inference as an onchain commodity. 

This is obviously a pro-sumer application; but that's fine because the largest winners of AI inference are individuals and small teams, not enterprises. Enterprises are either A) developing in-house model harnesses for privacy purposes, or B) have infinite budget for AI

And people treat that like a bear case - I don't see a problem with being for consumers. The TAM for consumer inference is still huge - Menlo Ventures State of Consumer AI est. 1.7b - 1.8b use AI tools ; at $20/m that's 432b a year. Also, in their enterprise report, product-led growth drives 27% of AI spend, and shadow AI (employees paying on their own) pushes that closer to 40%. Cursor hit $200M in revenue before hiring a single enterprise sales rep. 

There is a clear latent demand for cheap inference amongst pro-sumers. The unlocks are clear - it can become the payment layer for AI agents; More users buying credits leads to more demand for CREDIT, which makes staking ORBIO more valuable, which raises the ORBIO price, which creates more trading fees, which funds more discounts, which brings in more users. As long as it keeps spinning, each part feeds the others.

It combines three hot themes: AI agents, tokenized real-world assets, and Robinhood Chain. The NVDA-linked fee route adds to that. In a strong market, a story this clean can attract a lot of capital, which itself funds the subsidy for longer.

And of course, above it all, the man pushing this himself - @0x_aster is a cracked dev who has shown his capabililties are far beyond the norm; Multiple updates within a week, clear direction - this is founder-market fit. 

In crypto, actions carry way more weight than words. And look at what he's shipped man... a working gateway, a live orderbook, and now tokenized inference. The man is A MACHINE. This is what AI x strong founders can do - go beyond 10x engineer to become a 10,000x engineer. HE'S CRACKED!

Founder-market fit matters more in this sector than most. A team that ships slowly gets left behind by the market itself. 

And for the bear takes:

Q: DIEM already does this, why do we need another one

- DIEM is precisely the success case. VVV is valued at 1B. ORBIO is valued at 15m. Also, VVV is going in the direction of private AI. ORBIO is going in the direction of serving the layer of inference for consumers across the world. CREDIT is $1 of usage you hold until you need it. Burst-heavy users (agents running a big job, devs shipping a feature) don't use the same amount every day. They need compute they can stockpile, buy at a discount, and spend in one go.

Lastly, markets rarely have one winner. Stablecoins didn't stop at USDT. Venice proved people will pay for tokenized inference. There is room for a second design.

Q: It's just an OpenRouter reseller. There's no moat.

Fair take. Yes, bits can be copied, there's no moat there. The moat is the market - liquidity begets liquidity in any marketplace. There's 20 different perp dexes. Who wins? The most liquid markets with the most volume traded on it. 

And obv there is no confirmed answer, but ultimately, that's what markets are - I'm betting on this

Q: "They could be shut down"

This is the most legitimate bear take, yes. Platform risk is real for any aggregator. But labs want volume, and resellers bring demand they wouldn't otherwise get. Venice has run Claude, GPT and Gemini through a token model at scale, which suggests it can work.

But on top of that, as the world moves towards open source, this becomes less and less of a risk ;

Coinbase CEO：CLARITY法案未能推进，SEC与CFTC将推动加密监管明确化

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong表示，CLARITY法案今日未能在美国参议院推进，令人失望，但加密行业不能继续等待国会。

他称，SEC和CFTC已具备在现有授权下制定明确规则的工具，预计将着手推进相关工作。Armstrong还表示，GENIUS法案已为稳定币确立法律框架，尽管CLARITY法案未能通过，加密行业的监管清晰度仍将到来。
author: PANewsCN
quoted_text:
The CLARITY Act didn't advance in the Senate today, which was a disappointment. While it's possible bi-partisan conversations continue and it lives to fight another day, we can't wait on Congress anymore.

The SEC and CFTC have the tools they need to create clear rules under existing authority, and I expect will begin working on this in earnest.

So clarity is coming to crypto regardless.

And of course GENIUS is already the law of the land for stablecoins, which is even more permissive on rewards. There were some concessions we made on CLARITY that were tough to swallow, so perhaps it's for the best. 

Crypto can't be uninvented. With clarity emerging through the regulators, we'll continue updating the financial system.

Last month I wrote about how we can build a positive and safe future for everyone: https://t.co/eoLGVY8yad

Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens.

The reality is:

- People won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask, so labs have a strong natural incentive to make their models more aligned.

There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up. My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind.

- Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.

Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us. I'm proud of the security foundations we've built.

- Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice. MSL already does this today in several areas because it helps produce better work. Other labs can just do this too. In general, it would be helpful for there to be a larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators.

- Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely. Meta has made this commitment and other labs can do this as well.

I believe the key to building a positive future for everyone is maintaining the right balance of power. This is within our power to do.

text:
Li Lu’s story reads like a movie script.

He grew up in China. Became a student leader in the democracy movement. Stood in Tiananmen Square when the tanks rolled in. Fled the country as the CCP crushed the protests and started a new life in America with no money and no home to go back to.

“I didn’t know anybody,” he said, “and I didn’t have a penny to my name.”

Two years later, a classmate at Columbia Business School — who understood the young refugee’s financial struggles — told him about a speaker coming to campus who supposedly knew how to make money. Li Lu agreed to tag along. In large part because he heard the word “buffet” and assumed the lecture came with a free meal.

“To my dismay,” he later told the Graham & Doddsville newsletter, “there was no lunch. There was just a guy with the name Buffett.”

Empty stomach aside, that day changed the entire trajectory of Li Lu’s life. Buffett’s words hit him like “a punch in my eyes” and he was, forever after, in love with value investing.

Fast-forwarding a bit, he graduated and went on to found Himalaya Capital, earned Charlie Munger’s trust so completely that the legendary investor handed over a chunk of his own family’s fortune for Li Lu to manage, and was (for many years) even considered the odds-on favorite to one day run Berkshire Hathaway’s stock portfolio.

Li Lu shared this story — and many other thoughts and opinions — in a 2013 interview with the Graham & Doddsville newsletter (published by students in the Value Investing Program at Columbia Business School) and, for my money, it remains one of the best windows into the mind of this fascinating man. https://t.co/bEt4SJFbkH

text:
Peter Thiel 又要开一轮敌基督讲座了。

这次在 Nashville，9 月 28 日开始，连续四个周一。还是闭门、off the record，不能用设备，要查包和安检，具体地点直到前一天才告诉参加者。

主办方 The Pamphleteer 说，Thiel 会从历史、文学、艺术、神学和政治，一直讲到科学与技术的前沿。

他已经从旧金山一路讲到巴黎、罗马，现在又去了 Nashville。我觉得这基本就是他给自己整套政治和技术观搭出来的一套神学解释。

去年旧金山那四场后来漏出来很多内容，而且越看越离谱。

第一场他讲 Knowledge shall be increased。

核心逻辑是，21 世纪的敌基督可能不会靠战争夺权，反而会不断告诉所有人核战争、AI、气候灾难马上就要毁灭世界，然后要求人类为了和平与安全交出更多权力，最后控制科学和技术。

所以在他的框架里，Eliezer Yudkowsky、Nick Bostrom、Greta Thunberg 这些天天警告技术或者气候风险的人，甚至成了敌基督的军团。

第二场更有意思。他从《但以理书》开始讲全球化和帝国，又拿《新亚特兰蒂斯》《格列佛游记》《Watchmen》，甚至《海贼王》来解释不同版本的科技、政府和世界国家。

讲到最后还是那件事。Thiel 几乎把敌基督和 one-world state 放在一起。联合国、ICC、跨国监管机构，在他的世界观里都有往这个方向滑的可能。

第三场研究一个很 Thiel 的问题。

《圣经》说敌基督是一个人，一个普通人怎么可能在一辈子里统治全世界？

他的答案里居然有年龄、财富和速度。敌基督必须足够年轻，钱尤其重要，因为 money has this remarkable velocity。

他甚至花了不少时间研究为什么 33 岁这个数字反复出现在耶稣、佛陀、亚历山大和文学人物身上。

到了最后一场，他开始找今天的罗马。

美国既可能是阻止敌基督出现的 katechon，也可能是未来世界国家的起点。他尤其担心华盛顿的政治权力和旧金山的技术权力真正合流，觉得这会形成一种很危险的 Caesar-Papist fusion。

然后事情开始变得很幽默。

第一场刚讲完，一个叫 Kshitij Kulkarni 的听众把笔记发到了网上，马上被主办方取消了剩下三场的票，而且不退款。后来《华盛顿邮报》和《卫报》干脆拿到了四场讲座的录音，原本设计成 off the record 的整套理论基本被扒了出来。

再后来他把这一套带去了罗马，而且直接讲到了梵蒂冈门口。

这次反应就没旧金山那么客气了。几家被传与活动有关的天主教机构赶紧撇清关系。给教宗提供 AI 问题建议的神父 Paolo Benanti 直接把 Thiel 称作 Silicon Valley 的政治神学家，并把他的思想描述成一场针对自由主义共识的持续异端行为。

他把现实世界里非常具体的利益冲突，重新包装成了一场末日神学。

AI 到底需不需要监管，科技公司应该接受多少公共约束，国际机构有没有资格限制资本和技术，这些原本都可以正常争论。

进了 Thiel 的框架以后，性质全变了。

监管技术的人可能在替敌基督铺路，讨论 AI 灭绝风险的人可能是敌基督的军团，国际治理再往前一步，后面可能就是 one-world state。

政治分歧被直接抬成了善恶和末日问题。

更微妙的是，Thiel 对权力集中的警惕一直非常有方向感。

他会反复担心联合国、ICC、AI 监管和全球治理变得太强，却长期参与建设 Palantir。后者的软件深入美国国防、情报和移民执法体系，Thiel 自己也一直处在科技资本和华盛顿政治网络的交界处。

所以我现在再看他讲敌基督，最有意思的问题已经变成了另一个。

为什么国际机构获得更多权力，是通往敌基督；科技公司和国家机器把数据、AI、战争能力越来越紧密地接在一起，却可以被解释成阻止敌基督的力量？

这套理论对 Thiel 自己实在太方便了。

它可以把约束他的力量写进末日预言，又把他自己正在积累的力量留在预言之外。

author: gregosuri
quoted_text:
Last month I wrote about how we can build a positive and safe future for everyone: https://t.co/eoLGVY8yad

Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens.

The reality is:

- People won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask, so labs have a strong natural incentive to make their models more aligned.

There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up. My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind.

- Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.

Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us. I'm proud of the security foundations we've built.

- Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice. MSL already does this today in several areas because it helps produce better work. Other labs can just do this too. In general, it would be helpful for there to be a larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators.

- Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely. Meta has made this commitment and other labs can do this as well.

I believe the key to building a positive future for everyone is maintaining the right balance of power. This is within our power to do.

中国有句话：往者不可谏，来者犹可追。

特朗普发过 Meme、家族做了 World Liberty Financial，也确实从 Crypto 生意里获得了巨额收益。这些都是已经发生的事，不可能从历史里删掉。

现在共和党想解决的是：既然过去改不了，那就把规则补上，给美国 Crypto 的未来先立一个监管框架。

但沃伦的逻辑完全不同。

只要特朗普现有的 Crypto 利益还在，只要未来还有继续获利的可能，那么过去就不是“过去”，而是今天仍然存在的利益冲突。

所以共和党不管怎么改伦理条款，她都可以继续追问一句：这能不能真正阻止特朗普从 Crypto 赚钱？

这就是 CLARITY 最难解的死结。

一边觉得已经改了 126 项、特朗普也接受了大部分伦理限制，不能因为一个人的历史，把整个美国 Crypto 监管继续拖下去。

另一边认为，如果连总统本人和家族现有的 Crypto 利益都约束不了，那这部法案从根上就不完整。

最新版确实已经加入更严格的官员利益限制，但 Warren 等民主党人仍认为执法机制存在漏洞。

所以现在争的已经不是再改三条还是五条。

真正的分歧是：美国要不要先解决特朗普这个历史遗留问题，才有资格讨论 Crypto 的未来。

只要特朗普的 Crypto 生意还在，这个伦理问题就很难真正翻篇。

author: mykcryptodev
quoted_text:
TypeSafe just priced output tokens at zero.

Input is $0.042 per million tokens, per the launch. Every yes or no from a language model arrives inside a sentence it had to write one token at a time, and you pay for the whole sentence. Pricing output at zero follows from a model that writes almost none of it.

Diogo's launch post has the mechanism, and the waitlist. TypeSafe says Jev, its first public System One Model, answers many structured questions at once and returns a typed decision with a probability attached, so the calling code decides what happens next.

So an LLM call becomes something your code can branch on directly.

The launch example is support tickets. One long prompt splits into the judgments the app needs, is this urgent, is it billing, does it need a human? Each answer comes back typed with a confidence score, you pick a threshold, and anything under it goes to a person.

TypeSafe's phrase for it is smart if statements.

The confidence number is the piece I'd watch. Cheap tokens were never the whole blocker, since an output you have to double check still waits on a human before it touches production data. A probability that holds up the way TypeSafe describes would be the signal for when to let things run unattended.

Once a judgment is cheap and legible it lands in form handlers, notification checks, and every small place nobody would have written a prompt for. Threshold tuning turns into a real engineering skill, and the teams who learn it early automate the boring half of their stack.

author: sequoia
quoted_text:
Well.. @levie and I filmed this episode of Training Data a week or two ago, when the “current thing” was Doug Leone’s novacaine root canals instead of pacing the frontier… Simpler times!

But Aaron’s advice on reinventing yourself and your company for AI is timeless.

Aaron founded @Box 20 years ago. It sits on hundreds of billions of enterprise files, and he's bet the company on agents that can read every one of them. He's also one of the most wired-in people in AI, on every cap table and, by his own admission, 95% Twitter-educated. He’s the rare CEO who can straddle both the internet AND has the ear of CIOs.

His core argument: (1) the gap between what a model can do and what an enterprise workflow actually needs is vast, and closing it is a lot of software; (2) diffusion of AI outside of coding will take far longer than Silicon Valley thinks, and that slowness is exactly where the applied layer's value comes from.

The conversation covers:

— why application companies are the hottest neolabs, and why the LLM-wrapper thesis is finally working
 — the fox-guarding-the-henhouse problem with letting model providers route your tokens
 — work slop, and why we accept AI-written code but flinch at AI-written decks
 — how Box built its agentic harness and why it beats raw API access on accuracy and latency
 — the open-weights paradox: closed labs and open models both growing exponentially at once
 — what continual learning has to solve before it works for a lawyer with five matters and a Chinese wall
 — why 90% of enterprise tokens in five years will come from tasks no human kicked off
 — the mandate for founders right now: whoever gets it to the customer wins

0:00 – Introduction
1:55 – Are application companies the hottest neolabs?
6:56 – Will the labs move up the stack?
12:34 – Box and betting the company on AI
16:50 – Hero use cases: reading a million contracts and long-running agents
18:42 – Work slop: why AI code is embraced but AI content isn't
24:08 – Building Box's agentic harness and the evals that matter
27:23 – The state of the model race
29:25 – Open-weight model adoption in the enterprise
32:34 – Memory, continual learning, and what belongs in the weights
37:29 – Box Labs and systems of record in a world of agents
44:55 – Will chat be the dominant UI for enterprise AI?
48:00 – Why coding diffused fast and the rest of knowledge work hasn't
54:31 – Staying wired in, making a company AI-first, and what it takes to win

I was encouraged this week to see the leaders of the frontier labs agree on the need for them to slow down the pace of AI development. Given the stakes, it’s a good and necessary first step.
 
But I’m even more encouraged by the growing recognition that how this powerful new technology develops should be at the center of our public debate.
 
I’ve been watching the progress on AI for over a decade now, and one thing that’s clear to me is that the potential impact of this technology is not overhyped. It’s also moving at lightning speed – and even faster than those who are engineering it can keep up with.
 
I’m not an AI accelerationist who believes it will lead to some techno-utopia, and I’m not a doomer who thinks it will inevitably lead to humanity’s destruction.

But whether this technology results in amazing breakthroughs in medicine, energy and education or unleashes huge economic disruptions, greater inequality, and potential catastrophe will depend on the choices that we make right now – choices that should be made not just by the companies involved, but by all of us.

text:
With @standard_rsv now live, the real question is: what’s the thesis?

I’m seeing a lot of posts on my timeline claiming they pulled 5–6 figures from $STANDARD issuance via their Genesis NFTs, but is that actually true?

Quick reminder: RSV’s proposed design combines a reserve treasury with an unusual issuance system.

Participants hold charters and operate “branches” that accrue $STANDARD. Opening more branches requires buying licenses with $STANDARD, which gets burned.

To collect rewards, bankers retire a branch and sacrifice its future earning power. Withdrawal fees rise as more participants leave, rewarding those who remain.

The idea is clever: make expansion consume tokens, and make cashing out carry an opportunity cost.

Issuance also responds to net ETH flows.

Expansion directs resources toward reserves and liquidity; contraction shifts support toward buybacks. But reduced issuance still means potential dilution, and unminted rewards remain future supply.

Some potential Bear Cases:

- Reflexive demand risk
Nothing creates outside demand for $standard: bankers buy for licenses, speculators buy because bankers buy. If that’s the whole loop, it’s ohm with better plumbing.

- The signal is gameable
Net ETH flow drives “expansion.” A whale can push the pool, farm the multiplier/story, then dump. Smoothing and rate-limited buybacks slow it, don’t stop it. Day-one flow was boosted by launch/sniper/tax churn, not durable demand.

- Hidden float can flood the market
Branch balances aren’t circulating until withdrawal. Float can look tight, then big charter exits dump into an AMM that can’t absorb it. Fees tax exits but don’t cap sell pressure, especially with concentrated ownership.

- Complexity adds failure modes
Hooks, auctions, exit fees, dormancy, two vaults, and book-then-mint introduce more edge cases than a plain ERC-20. Audits find bugs; they don’t prove it will hold up in a risk-off, thin L2. The team still takes 15% of fee ETH. Some reserve execution appears to be owner-gated.

The Bull Cases:

- OHM’s failure wasn’t rebranded, it was patched.
Olympus printed high APY on a schedule; when inflows stopped, dilution turned into sell pressure.Standard Reserve ties issuance to net ETH flow through a single Uniswap v4 pool. It cuts the multiplier immediately on negative flow, and only raises it after two straight positive epochs. Fees switch by regime: gold + POL on the way up, buybacks + burns on the way down.

- The “banker loop” is a real supply sink.
For incumbents, the best move, buying expansion licenses to open branches, burns 100% of $STANDARD. You can’t keep the yield source. Retiring a branch mints tokens but destroys the future claim; the final branch burns the charter. Exit fees rise with withdrawal pressure (~2% in calm to ~60% in a run), split half burned and half paid to stayers, turning bank runs on their head.

If the flywheel works: ETH inflows → higher m → issuance to bankers who expand (more burns) → fees stack gold + POL → thicker reserves → more charter demand. New charters pay ETH into the same engine, so adoption strengthens reserves.

That makes early access to freshly minted STANDARD fairly tough, tightening supply at first, but as the cycle keeps running and minting ramps up, more tokens should hit circulation and the price may settle into balance.

NFA. DYOR.
author: Eli5defi
quoted_text:
Onchain experimentation is getting interesting again, and @standard_rsv is one of the more unusual designs I’ve seen recently.

At first glance, it has some OlympusDAO vibes. Under the hood, it’s almost the inverse.

---

Here's the quick breakdown:

Standard Reserve is basically an autonomous onchain central bank. Instead, it run the entire monetary system around one currency, one market, and one signal:

$STANDARD + an @Uniswap v4 $ETH - $STANDARD pool + $ETH flow.

STANDARD has a 1B hard cap:

- 100M starts as permanent protocol-owned liquidity
- 900M forms the remaining issuance budget
- Multiple mechanisms continuously burn the supply

The interesting part is how monetary policy reacts.

- ETH flowing in → expansion.

Issuance can gradually increase, while protocol revenue accumulates reserves such as tokenized gold.

- ETH flowing out → contraction.

Issuance gets cut faster, the vault starts buying $STANDARD from the market, and those tokens are burned.

And then you have the “bankers.”

Standard Reserve launches with 1,000 Founding Charters, initially soulbound NFTs representing banking licenses (minting soon).

Each Charter starts with 1 Branch, expandable to a maximum of 10.
Each Branch earns an equal share of protocol issuance.

Want more earning power? You need an Expansion License.

Around 100 licenses/day are auctioned in STANDARD, with a maximum of 3 per Charter per day.

And 100% of the STANDARD paid gets burned.

This creates the first flywheel:

Issuance → demand for Branches → STANDARD spent → STANDARD burned → larger future issuance share.

But there’s another catch.

You cannot simply harvest forever. To realize the STANDARD earned by a Branch, you must retire it permanently.

Your tokens are minted, the Branch disappears, and you pay a dynamic resolution fee based on system-wide exit pressure over the previous 7 days.

Simply put, the more people rushing for the exit, the more expensive exiting becomes.

Of that fee:

- 50% is burned.
- 50% goes to bankers who stayed.

Meanwhile, every swap and new Charter auction generates ETH fees:

- 70% → active reserve vault
- 15% → permanent liquidity
- 15% → team

Put everything together and you get a pretty unusual closed-loop economy:

ETH inflows → issuance rises → bankers compound → STANDARD burns → reserves/POL grow

Then when flows reverse:

ETH outflows → issuance falls → buybacks activate → STANDARD burns → exits reward remaining bankers

---

Personally, if the design works, monetary policy becomes a mechanical response to real capital flows: expansion when demand is strong, contraction when it weakens, and structural burns everywhere in between.

Pretty interesting, I’m looking forward to their NFTs mint and mainnet launch.

NFA. DYOR.
